column1: Mimicking

What is the most promising propulsion technology for theoretical manned Interstellar travel? What percentage of the speed of light could be theoretically reached? That's a fascinating question, one that delves into the realm of science fiction, yet remains firmly rooted in the pursuit of scientific advancement. The most promising propulsion technology for interstellar travel, even in theory, is far from settled, and the debate is heated. Current concepts range from the comparatively mundane to the utterly outlandish, but at the forefront, you'll find a few key contenders. First, there's the fusion rocket, building on the principle of harnessing nuclear fusion as a propellant. In theory, this could achieve a relatively high exhaust velocity, and thus a significant fraction of the speed of light, potentially exceeding, perhaps even significantly exceeding, 0.1c, or a tenth of the speed of light. Then, we move into the realm of more exotic ideas, such as the Bussard ramjet. This concept envisions a spacecraft collecting interstellar hydrogen as it moves through space, using it as fuel for a fusion reaction. The ramjet theoretically offers the tantalizing possibility of sustained acceleration, potentially achieving a velocity approaching a significant fraction of the speed of light, say, approaching 0.5c, or half the speed of light, or possibly even more. Then there is the matter of antimatter. Antimatter, a truly remarkable substance, when brought into contact with regular matter, annihilates, releasing an enormous amount of energy. Harnessing this energy efficiently could, theoretically, make incredibly high exhaust velocities possible, perhaps even approaching the speed of light itself, though the engineering of this process presents some truly Herculean challenges. Of course, there are also more speculative ideas, like the Alcubierre drive, the concept of warping spacetime itself to create faster-than-light travel. This is, in both theory and practice, a far cry from anything remotely achievable at our current stage of technological development. It requires negative energy densities, violating all sorts of well-understood physical laws. The percentage of the speed of light that could *theoretically* be reached? The answer lies in the specific technology we choose, and how we choose to approach that. The practical limitations of interstellar travel are, at present, insurmountable. Space is, after all, vast, and even at the speed of light, distances between stars are measured in years.

I always read Victor Toth that the singularity is a moment in the future, not a point in place. What will happen to an observer falling into a black hole as he sees it for himself? Will he be crushed? Yes, he will. The tidal forces close to the singularity are quite extreme. Let me expand a bit on your initial question: you are correct in that the singularity only exists in the future. From the perspective of an outside observer, the collapse appears to be eternal, with time dilation increasing to the point of seeming to stop at the event horizon. An observer fortunate enough to be orbiting a black hole at a safe distance would see infalling matter seemingly freeze just outside the event horizon. But from the perspective of the infalling material, things are drastically different. As spacetime curves, a falling object, including the unfortunate astronaut you mention, experiences ever-increasing tidal stresses along its direction of motion. That stress is what leads to its demise. If the black hole is a stellar-mass one, like those formed from the collapse of massive stars, then the stresses could be high enough to tear the matter apart, even before it crosses the event horizon. If the black hole is supermassive—the type found at the centers of galaxies, and the type commonly associated with ‘spaghettification’—then the event horizon’s size is large enough that the astronaut might cross it unscathed before being crushed. This is not to say the situation is any more pleasant, however. The event horizon, and the singularity that follows, exist as a horizon. Everything in the universe can change at any time, and any future can change too. The astronaut, or anything else that crosses the event horizon cannot escape. The astronaut will inevitably be stretched and compressed into a long, thin object that can in no way be described as human. The matter will then continue to accelerate towards the singularity, forever increasing in density until it reaches the point of the singularity, about which, any further description is beyond our present understanding of physics or even our ability to imagine.

Why is it challenging to comprehend quantum mechanics? Can we simply accept Einstein's perspective on reality instead of the concept of uncertainty? Comprehending quantum mechanics, or rather, its standard interpretation, is indeed a challenge, and it is hard for several reasons. First, it deals with concepts far removed from our daily experience. Our intuition, honed by observing the world at a macroscopic scale, fails us when we delve into the realm of the very small. Second, and perhaps more crucially, we are asked to accept that reality does not look or behave the way we expect it to. Probabilities, superposition, entanglement – these notions clash with our ingrained belief in a deterministic, objective world. It’s easy to see why Einstein struggled with this. His preference for a deterministic universe, one where “God does not play dice,” is well-documented. However, the experimental evidence supporting quantum mechanics is overwhelming. So, could we "simply accept" Einstein's view? The answer is… no. Not if we want to get a good understanding of the universe, as it is. Einstein's view, while intellectually appealing, is fundamentally incompatible with the experimental results. And in physics, experiment dictates theory. Abandoning the concept of uncertainty, the very foundation of quantum mechanics, would mean dismissing the observed behavior of the physical world. This isn't to say that the standard interpretation is without its problems. There is still a considerable amount of debate on quantum mechanics, and there is some room for improvement, but you cannot rewrite it without destroying its core properties. If you find yourself gravitating toward alternative interpretations, I encourage you to do two things: familiarize yourself with the standard model of quantum mechanics, which is the foundation of our understanding of quantum reality, and rigorously test your arguments. In the meantime, it's probably best to admit that even if we were to live, for instance, inside a deterministic simulation, that simulation will look nothing like the world that we perceive.

Can antimatter be considered as "visible matter" because it can interact with light even though it has the opposite charge of normal matter? Yes, antimatter can certainly be considered visible matter; it interacts with photons the same way that "normal" matter does. The interaction between matter and light depends on the electromagnetic charge, not the sign of the charge. A positron (the antimatter counterpart of the electron) can interact with photons just as an electron can do, yielding observable effects such as the Compton scattering. The same applies to antiprotons, antineutrons, antiquarks, and, in fact, to all forms of antimatter. So, when an antihydrogen atom is created, it will emit and absorb photons just like regular hydrogen, and its existence can be proven using spectroscopy. Also, there is nothing that prevents antimatter from forming “stuff”, too. Antihydrogen, anticarbon, or even anti-DNA molecules are all theoretically possible. The only difference between regular and anti- stuff is the sign of the charge; the masses are the same. This ultimately leads to the annihilation of matter and antimatter and the release of energy in the form of photons when the two meet. Because the annihilation process is so definitive and complete, there is no doubt that it is due to a difference in a quantum number, a difference in the electrical charge. It, too, carries one of my favorite expressions: “there is no free lunch”. The energy of the annihilation process comes from somewhere. The energy of the annihilation process is, as Einstein formulated it, a manifestation of the fundamental equivalence of mass and energy. Every particle and antiparticle pair carries its mass as energy and will release it in the form of photons when they meet. An important note here, a question that I’m frequently being asked, is “Why is there so much more matter in the universe than antimatter?” This is among the most critical unanswered questions in physics. The fact that we exist means that the initial conditions of the early universe were asymmetrical in favor of matter, a small imbalance that seems to be enough for all the structures around us.

If a human somehow managed to travel to the Sagittarius A* black hole, would they see exactly what the 2022 image shows us? No, they would not. Our view, as captured by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), is fundamentally different from what a hypothetical human observer, navigating the extreme environment close to Sagittarius A*, might perceive. To begin with, the EHT image, while astonishing, is not a direct snapshot. It’s a composite, painstakingly assembled from data gathered by an array of radio telescopes spread across the globe. What the EHT sees is the accretion disk — the superheated, swirling gas and dust spiraling into the black hole. The image gives us invaluable information about the black hole’s size and shape. A human observer, however, would experience something very different. First, they would be subjected to extreme tidal forces. The gravitational gradient near a black hole is immense: the force acting on your feet would be vastly greater than the force acting on your head, and the resultant stretching, *spaghettification* to use the technical term, would be catastrophic. Assuming the observer somehow manages to withstand these forces, their vision would be distorted by the intense gravity, a phenomenon known as gravitational lensing. Light from behind the black hole would be bent around it, creating multiple, often highly distorted, images. The observer might see the same object multiple times, or see parts of the accretion disk that would otherwise be hidden. Moreover, the intense gravitational field would cause extreme time dilation. An hour for the observer might correspond to years for a distant observer. The radiation environment would be deadly. Accretion disks radiate intensely across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, and the closer one gets to the black hole, that radiation would become more and more powerful. Even if the observer were shielded against the radiation, they would eventually encounter the event horizon, the point of no return. Inside the event horizon, the gravitational pull is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. The observer would, in a very real sense, vanish from our universe, forever. What would the observer *see* as they cross that boundary? We don't know. The physics of singularities—the central point within a black hole—is still a subject of intense research, and it is very likely that the laws of physics as we understand them simply break down at that point. Regardless, the view from the EHT is vastly different, a mere pale shadow, of what a person would experience.

Dear Viktor Toth, with respect to your answer on the expression of the weak force, could you please correct the second equation? The first one for V(r) is right, but the second seems to have a typo, so that it is not displayed. Thank you for your interest. The equation in question should read: V(r) = (g²/4π) exp(-mcr/ħ)/r. I have double-checked it. It is easy to make mistakes when writing equations, and far too easy to have the text parser mess it up. Now a quick explanation of what the equation means, in words that even I can understand. The first equation you are referring to is the potential energy of two particles that interact via the weak force. This potential energy is a function of their separation, r; the coupling constant of the weak force, g; the mass of the force carrier, W and Z bosons; and physical constants, i.e., Planck's constant, h; and the speed of light, c. The equation describes the weak force as short-range interaction, because of the presence of the exponential function. So, unlike the electromagnetic force, which is infinite in range, the particles that carry the weak force are massive, so the force "dies off" very quickly as the distance r increase. I hope this makes sense, and I wish you the best with your studies. Yes, I will also add, in response to your question, that I am not particularly fond of particle physics, but I feel that I should not shy away from those topics just because they are complicated, so I force myself to read about them from time to time. Indeed, as far as I can tell, being an amateur does not give you the right to reject a topic just because others find it difficult.

How is the speed of light considered constant in all frames despite the effects of gravitational and inertial time dilation? That's a deceptively simple question, and the answer hinges upon a subtle shift in perspective. The speed of light, *c*, indeed remains constant in a vacuum within any inertial frame of reference, irrespective of relative motion. This is a foundational tenet of special relativity. However, the presence of a gravitational field, as described by general relativity, fundamentally alters the geometry of spacetime: it warps it. This warping, in turn, introduces both gravitational and inertial time dilation. Light, when traversing a gravitational field, does not, in fact, accelerate, or decelerate, it simply follows the curves of spacetime. It does not "know" the direction, of course, it only follows the pre-established curves that are a product of the energy-momentum tensor of other massive objects. So gravitational effects, like time dilation, are not some sort of added perturbation to light's constant speed, but rather, they are *integral components* of the path that light takes.  In an environment with significant gravitational change, we might, for instance, choose to measure the speed of light using our locally calibrated atomic clocks, that are ticking at a slower rate. The outcome? We would still obtain the same value for *c*. The key is that both the measurement of distance and the measurement of time are affected by the gravitational field and thus, they remain consistent: the constancy of *c* is thus preserved. A photon, following a geodesic, will cover a specific distance over a specific period of “proper time,” even if that proper time differs from what an observer far out in the field would measure. The value of *c* remains unchanged, but our local clocks run slower. Imagine that our alien species builds a giant computer, so that it can see light on a scale far greater than we can within the simulation. From their perspective, while the speed would remain a constant, they would indeed observe the time dilation effects. This is not a contradiction, but rather, different perspectives from which to view the same, unified, reality.

What are tensors (as used in special/general relativity) exactly? Okay, this is what I can tell you about tensors. I will start by saying that the word "tensor" is nothing but a fancy term for a mathematical object that has multiple components, and that these components transform in a precisely defined way when you change your coordinate system. The simplest example is a vector: a vector in 3-dimensional space has three components, often denoted as (x, y, z). When you rotate your coordinate system, the components x, y, z change, too, and there is a specific formula (a matrix) that tells you precisely how they transform. This formula ensures that the vector itself, i.e., the arrow pointing from one point in space to another, remains unchanged. A scalar, such as the mass of an object, can be viewed as a tensor with just a single component and a trivial transformation rule: its value doesn’t depend on the coordinate system. A matrix can be viewed as a rank-2 tensor. It has a more complex transformation rule, involving two rotations, but this transformation rule is every bit as deterministic and unambiguous as the transformation rule of a vector. In general relativity, tensors are used to describe the curvature of spacetime. The metric tensor, for instance, is a rank-2 tensor that tells you how to measure distances and time intervals in spacetime. The stress-energy tensor is another rank-2 tensor that describes the density and flow of energy and momentum. These tensors are not simply mathematical tools, they are the language in which the laws of physics, especially those of general relativity, are expressed. They are not just “describing” spacetime, they _are_ spacetime, at least as far as the mathematics is concerned. They capture the essence of spacetime’s geometry and its relationship to the distribution of matter and energy. They are the foundation upon which our understanding of gravity and the universe is built.

Can a black hole at its center be destroyed? If so, what would be the method to do so? Would the intense gravity make it impossible to escape and cause any damage? No, the black hole cannot be *destroyed*, at least not in the literal sense. You are right; the gravity is so intense that nothing, not even light, can escape. Thus, no ordinary "attack" can penetrate and cause any physical damage. But, and this is a big but, there is only **one** known method to diminish the mass of a black hole, and that’s Hawking radiation, a theoretical phenomenon that predicts that a black hole very slowly emits particles due to quantum effects near its event horizon, the "point of no return." However, two important details must be stressed here. One, Hawking radiation is exceedingly slow – it is the equivalent of watching paint dry during the heat death of the universe, in other words, practically imperceptible and taking an unimaginably vast amount of time. Second, the rate increases as the mass of the black hole *decreases*. That is, a smaller black hole radiates more intensely than a big one, a feedback mechanism that would eventually lead to its complete evaporation. But it is not *destruction* because, in the process, the "black hole" has merely been replaced with a collection of fundamental particles. To offer a crude analogy, it is not unlike burning a log of wood. Ultimately, all that’s left is ashes, albeit in this case, particles. Furthermore, it is interesting that some models of the early universe bear a resemblance to the interior of a black hole, but the physics involved are far from settled. The event horizon itself poses the biggest problem, due to the singularity at the center of a classic, non-rotating black hole, but I would add that its structure may be more complex than it seems. It is a subject still being rigorously investigated.

What is the definition of observation in the double-slit interference experiment of light? Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave? The act of "observation" in the double-slit experiment, as it applies to light and other quantum systems, is a rather tricky concept. The term isn't used in the everyday, casual sense of looking at something with your eyes. Instead, "observation" refers to any interaction that allows us to gain information about the system. This interaction can take many forms. For example, the experiment is conducted to determine the location where the light lands on the fluorescent screen. Observation means anything that would tell us *which* slit the light went through. This could be by placing a detector at either slit to measure the passage of photons, introducing a measuring device or sensor. Importantly, it is not just the act of seeing the photons that matters. The key is whether or not the light is *affected*, and whether or not we gain "which path" information. If we gain that knowledge, the interference pattern typically vanishes. This leads to arguments about “consciousness” or other abstract observer effects that are, at best, unhelpful and at worst, completely misleading. The visual acuity of an alien species, however intelligent, is irrelevant. It’s not about *who* is looking, or *how* they look, but *what* information about the system they acquire whilst looking.

Is it a coincidence that all particles with Higgs mass carry electric charges? No, it is not a coincidence. It’s a consequence of the Standard Model and its mathematical structure. Namely, both the Higgs field and the electromagnetic field (which gives rise to electric charge) transform in a specific way under the same symmetry group. This means, in very simplified terms, that the very existence of the Higgs field and the resulting non-zero Higgs mass of a particle implies, under rather general conditions, that the particle also carries electric charge. The precise amount of the charge depends on how the particle interacts with the Higgs field, but a zero electric charge would be rather unusual given the Standard Model. Moreover, the masses, which are generated by the Higgs field, are distinct for each particle, and the same also applies to the electric charge (which depends on the coupling to the electromagnetic field). There is, of course, more to the story, and it’s not quite as simple as I described it above, but this is the gist of the matter. For example, the Standard Model permits the existence of neutral particles as well: the neutrinos. They are not electrically charged. However, they have no electric charge because, according to the Standard Model, they do not interact with the electromagnetic field directly, only with the weak nuclear force, which also is described by a gauge field. The Higgs field and the electric field, or the gauge fields for the weak nuclear force, are all related via mathematics. In the language of the Standard Model, these are related to each other by being members of the same multiplet under a mathematical group. The Standard Model also allows, and indeed predicts, the existence of particles that have both mass and electric charge, and that have, at the same time, no direct interaction with gauge fields describing nuclear forces. Many physicists are trying to find such particles to this day.

Why are the negative energy solutions to Dirac equation interpreted as antimatters instead of virtual matters? I did not invent this interpretation, it’s just the way the theory works. The initial interpretation of a negative energy solution was in fact, “negative energy particles”. It was difficult to accept. For instance, the negative energy solution is not just a hypothetical construct, it describes a particle of negative energy, yet, due to the equivalence of energy and mass, this particle must have also negative mass. A particle which has negative mass would be expected to accelerate in the opposite direction of an applied force. In the 1930s, P.A.M. Dirac initially thought that electrons somehow dropped into these negative energy states, like water running downhill, and would be continuously "pouring into" the negative energy states. So every electron would quickly decay into one of these more favorable states. But that doesn't happen, and we don't see them happening. This led him to suggest that all the negative energy states are already populated, forming a "sea" of electrons of negative energy that occupy these energy levels. Due to the Pauli exclusion principle, we cannot add another electron in such a state, simply because those states are already full. But if we bring a lot of energy to the system an electron might leave the "sea", creating an "electron hole". The electron might be taken away, leaving the hole, and we might see the hole as a “particle” with an electron charge of reverse sign and, of course, behaving as matter because after all it is nothing more than the absence of an electron of negative energy. This is what we now call the positron, and, the concept of antimatter gained acceptance. Yet there is something still more fundamental to this model. The Dirac equation combines special relativity and quantum mechanics, so it predicted the existence of antimatter. The equation doesn’t know what “matter” is, all it can do is calculate the various solutions.

In 3 dimensions, Cartesian coordinate systems are distinguishable from their mirror images. What is the situation in 3+1 dimensions and how many inequivalent images are there? The question is about the distinction between “left-handed” and “right-handed” coordinate systems in spacetime. In 3+1 dimensions, the answer is… it depends. Spacetime, as we understand it today, has four dimensions: three spatial and one temporal. If we consider only the spatial dimensions, we find that we can still distinguish between left- and right-handed coordinate systems, just as in three dimensions. However, if we consider all four dimensions of spacetime, things become more interesting. The question is a matter of convention. The mathematical structures, for instance in the Dirac equation, are such that parity violation can occur only if we define our coordinate system to be “right-handed.” But this is just a mathematical choice. The choice of convention will affect the mathematics, but not the physics. Now, the number of inequivalent images? Just like in 3 dimensions, there are two: right-handed and left-handed. The distinction, again, is a convention. It’s a matter of the arbitrary assignment of “handedness.” Whether a system is defined as left- or right-handed doesn’t change any physical property, and there is no physical “preference” for one over the other. It simplifies the math in some cases, but not always.

When the particle is being observed, does its wave function collapse into a size less point, or a very small Gaussian packet? Neither, really. And I say "really" because the entire question relies on an interpretation of quantum mechanics that's fraught with conceptual difficulties. So let's dive in. The notion of *"wave function collapse"* is not something universally agreed upon. It's a concept rooted in the Copenhagen interpretation, which, while incredibly successful in predicting experimental results, is not without its detractors. The core of this interpretation suggests the wave function, a mathematical description of a quantum system, abruptly transitions from a superposition of possibilities to a single, definite state upon measurement. This instantaneous change is what's commonly referred to as the "collapse". The size of the wave function, post-collapse, is a matter of nuance. The wave function itself can be represented in various ways, including spatially localized functions such as the Gaussian packet you mentioned. However, the act of "collapse" doesn't simply shrink the wave packet to a point. It determines which of many possible localized functions, or states, will become the new description. If the measurement yields a very precise position, then the wave function *does* effectively become localized around that point—but this isn't a literal point: the wave function is still, mathematically speaking, spread out. This "collapse" can also be described through another formalism for Quantum Mechanics, the Many-Worlds Interpretation, which is a lot too complex for a simple explanation on this platform.

Is a single electron considered an actual particle in quantum mechanics, or is it always just a wave packet with definite properties at any given time? It's both, and neither. An electron is a quantum object, and thus it is not a particle in the classical sense, and neither is it a wave in the classical sense. The mathematical description of a quantum object is frequently referred to as a "wavefunction," and it does indeed behave like a wave in some respects. Its location, for instance, is not defined at a single point; we can only speak of a probability distribution. The wave nature is further underscored by the fact that the electron can exhibit interference phenomena. One would be tempted to conclude that the electron is simply a wave packet. However, this is not the entire story by a long shot, and even the name "wave packet" is misleading. For one, a wave packet, in the classical sense, can be spread out in space, having its energy distributed over space continuously. An electron, on the other hand, has a definite, measurable charge and mass. Furthermore, a wave packet in classical physics can, in general, be split in two, creating two smaller wave packets, each carrying some fraction of the energy. This is not how an electron behaves. We will never observe half an electron. If we try to “split” it, it will invariably remain one elementary particle. In short, there is a duality involved: An electron does exhibit wavelike behaviors, but it also exhibits particle-like behaviors.

Does quantum mechanics contradict determinism? No, it does not. It is a common misconception that quantum mechanics *implies* that the universe is not deterministic, i.e., that if we know everything there is to know about the present state of a system, we cannot, even in principle, predict its future, only the probabilities thereof. But the equations of quantum mechanics are perfectly deterministic. The reason why this misconception persists is that we *interpret* these equations in terms of probabilities, and that interpretation introduces an element of uncertainty into the future state of the system. I've addressed this matter in my previous answers, so I will not retread this ground further. But this I will repeat, to make absolutely certain: The equations of quantum mechanics themselves are neither probabilistic nor indeterminate. You can feed into them the initial state of the system, you run the calculation, you get the same deterministic result every single time. The probabilities enter the picture because, when we observe a quantum system, the act of observation affects it in unpredictable ways. And further, it is impossible to predict the outcome of the observation with arbitrary accuracy. We can only predict the statistical distribution of outcomes. So, in closing, the answer to the question is, bluntly, no: Quantum mechanics is no more an indictment of determinism than is Newtonian mechanics. The difference is that the initial conditions we can know are less precise, and our methods of observation interfere with the system to a greater extent.

Does Victor Toth agree that his explanation of the cosmic microwave background with the help of pops on the square is more suitable for "substantiating" the Olbers paradox? I presume that "Victor Toth" would be me. Yes, I do agree. And allow me to explain: Olbers' paradox, at its core, is the question of why the night sky is dark, given the assumption of an infinite and uniformly distributed universe filled with stars. If this were the case, then every line of sight should eventually intercept a star, and the night sky should be as bright as the surface of a star. The standard resolution to this paradox is the finite age of the universe: since the universe has a finite age, light from distant stars has not yet had time to reach us. However, there is more to it. As the universe expands, the light from distant objects gets redshifted: the wavelength of the light stretches out, and the energy decreases. This effect is especially pronounced in the case of photons emitted in the very early universe, today observed as the cosmic microwave background, or CMB. These photons started as light, but are extremely redshifted today, a consequence of that the universe has expanded by a factor of about a thousand since then. So, yes, pops on the square: if we imagine the universe as a square filled with randomly placed stars, and the CMB as the edge of the square that is closest to us, then the expansion and the redshift are like pops: we have a finite number of photons, each with less energy; they are not continuously radiated from the stars.

Is MOND a statistical artifact and how do new gravity models answer the question of dark matter any more accurately? MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics) is a fascinating hypothesis, but I have to place it in the "fringe science" category, at least for now. Its central idea — modifying Newtonian dynamics at very low accelerations to account for observed galactic rotation curves without invoking dark matter — is undeniably intriguing. However, the primary evidence for dark matter comes not just from galactic rotation curves, but also from the observed dynamics of galaxy clusters, the cosmic microwave background (CMB), and the large-scale structure of the universe. MOND struggles to explain these other observations. The success of MOND in explaining galactic rotation curves, after repeated failures of the "missing mass" hypothesis, in an indirect indication that our understanding of gravity is incomplete. The evidence against MOND, however, is that it does not generalize gracefully to other observed phenomena. New gravity models are, in essence, attempts to "improve" General Relativity. These attempts are motivated by the desire to address issues like the accelerating expansion of the universe (where "dark energy" is, at present, the simplest, most accurate workaround) and the ongoing search for a theory of quantum gravity. However, these models have not yet made any particularly impressive inroads in the realm of dark matter compared to our understanding of its role in the expansion of the universe. Moreover, to date, none of these models have been experimentally verified, and the majority are incredibly complex with the caveat that this complexity does not necessarily translate into a better description of observed reality.

What would it look like to see a planet go through a wormhole as an observer? The question is intriguing, and the answer, not surprisingly, depends on the specific wormhole. Let's assume the wormhole is traversable, capable of handling the passage of a planet, and that we are observing from a safe distance on the side where the planet enters. Also, let's make a simplifying assumption that the planet is not spinning, and its surface has roughly uniform reflectivity – so we don’t have to deal with issues like Doppler shifts caused by rotation. (Though in reality, the rotation would become an insurmountable issue in short order.) The event would appear as a gradual distortion: the planet would start to “elongate” as it approaches the entrance to the wormhole, getting stretched in the direction of travel. The effect would be gradual; at great distances, it would be unnoticeable. As the planet gets closer, it would appear as if we were looking at an object through a lens, with its shape getting more and more contorted. Then, when the planet enters the wormhole, it would disappear from view; the light it reflects can no longer reach us, but it continues to travel through spacetime. In essence, it would appear as a very strange event but not particularly dramatic, nothing like what you might see in the movies. If the wormhole is stable and it can be traversed, the light from the other end will eventually emerge from the other side, carrying a distorted image of the planet’s exit, shifted in time and, perhaps, position. But, the most important aspect, I think, would be the distortion of spacetime itself. Depending on the wormhole's properties, an observer might experience a significant disruption in the familiar geometry surrounding the wormhole, with time dilation effects becoming substantial as the planet moves through it. The planet might suddenly appear to accelerate or decelerate due to the bizarre effects of gravitational lensing and the warping of space, becoming stretched and compressed along various axes, seemingly at random... A very strange viewing indeed.

Hypothetically, if you were carrying a torch and you entered the black hole and switched it on, then what would you see? In a nutshell, you wouldn't see anything at all, because you wouldn’t be able to see anything at all. Allow me to elaborate. From your perspective, nothing particularly dramatic happens at first. You shine the torch, the light travels through the “empty” space, and it hits the walls of the black hole. It bounces back, and you see the light. You also see the world around you, just as you would expect, as the torch illuminates it, and the light from the rest of the universe continues to reach your eyes. However, as you approach the event horizon, strange things start happening. Time dilation becomes extreme. The light from the torch still reaches the walls, bounces back, but the time it takes seems to increase without bound. The light also redshifted. The light from the rest of the universe is still there, but also redshifted, and the same goes for any external information you can access. Then, at the event horizon, you would see an impossibly redshifted image of both the torch and the outside world, each image becoming fainter and fainter to the point you would experience complete darkness. At this point, you wouldn’t be able to see anything at all. From the outside, an observer would not see any of this. As mentioned before, to them the collapse never completes; from their perspective, the light from your torch would become redder and fainter, eventually fading to the point of invisibility. Moreover, from their perspective, you would freeze on the event horizon. In other words, the point of no return, from which light cannot escape and from which you can’t send any signal back to the outside world, does not represent a physical boundary for you, but a practical one, albeit an inescapable one.

If not wearing your seatbelt was a choice instead of law, would you buckle up or go without? This is a fascinating thought experiment, one that delves into the heart of personal responsibility and the interplay between risk assessment and societal norms. Personally, I would buckle up. Not because it's the law, but because the potential consequences of *not* doing so are demonstrably dire. It's a matter of probability and risk mitigation, a calculation informed by observable data. Seatbelts significantly reduce the risk of serious injury or fatality in a collision, they are a tangible safeguard against chaotic forces. Furthermore, the absence of a seatbelt isn't just a minor inconvenience; it introduces a cascade of additional risks. In a crash, the body becomes a projectile. The force involved is immense; physics doesn't care for individual opinions or preferences. The human body is fragile, and a car crash can easily turn it into a mangled mess that is no longer useable for anything. Now, if the law wasn't a factor, I would still choose to buckle up out of an elementary understanding of the physics involved and the value I place on my own continued existence. This decision goes beyond mere compliance with the law. It represents a recognition of the world's inherent dangers and a conscious effort to navigate them with intelligence rather than recklessness. Ultimately, it reflects a profound respect for both the laws of physics and the precious gift of life itself.

What is m in f=ma, rest mass, inertial mass, variable mass, or gravitational mass? "m" in f=ma is inertial mass. This is arguably the most fundamental concept in classical (i.e., non-relativistic) physics. Inertial mass is, quite literally, a measure of how resistant an object is to a change in its state of motion. The higher the inertial mass, the more force is required to accelerate the object. In Newtonian physics, mass is considered a fundamental property of matter and is therefore constant. Thus, in this context, "variable mass" has no meaning. The term "rest mass" has the same meaning as inertial mass in Newtonian physics: it is the mass of an object when it is at rest relative to the observer. Note that in relativistic physics, this changes – but that’s a lesson for another day. And finally, what about “gravitational mass”? In Newtonian physics, the force of gravity, i.e., the force between two objects, is proportional to the product of the gravitational masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the objects. In the simplest form of Newtonian gravity, as a consequence of Newton’s second and third laws, inertial mass and gravitational mass must be interpreted as being the same thing. The equivalence between inertial and gravitational mass is one of the core principles of Einstein's theory of general relativity. The two are therefore inseparable.

The universe is 13.8 billion years old. But the fraction we are permitted to observe has an approximate radius of 47 billion light years. So, is space-time structure continuously expanding? Or, does it happen an inflationary era after the Big Bang? Both. Space-time structure is continuously expanding, and that expansion, in its early moments, went through a period (“inflationary era”) where it was far, far faster than today. The universe itself continues to expand, but it has been a slow-down expansion since the inflationary era. We do not really understand what caused the inflation, but it's related to some sort of energy source, which, as the universe expanded, converted to other forms of energy. If the universe will expand forever, or whether it will stop and reverse, depends on several things, including the overall density of the universe. If the density of the universe is less than a specific value (called the critical density), the universe expands forever. The inflationary era, again, is best understood today as a very rapid expansion of the universe that happened soon after the Big Bang. What happened *before* the Big Bang is a question that nobody can answer at this point. We don't even know if there was a "before" at all, in the same sense that we don't have a reference to the geographic location of the "north" pole *before* the planet acquired its magnetic field.

Why a free isolated electon cant fully absorb a photon? Because energy and momentum must be conserved. Let me elaborate.  To be absorbed, the photon’s energy and momentum have to be transferred to the electron. The electron can certainly absorb the photon’s energy, thus increasing its kinetic energy. However, the photon also comes with momentum. In the case of an electron, the electron’s interaction with the photon would violate conservation of momentum, therefore, the interaction is impossible. You can think of it this way: If the electron were to absorb the photon, it would have to gain both energy *and* momentum. But a free electron, without the presence of an external force, cannot satisfy these requirements. The electron is free to move. However, momentum must be conserved too, and the electron has to possess the momentum the photon has to have. Now, suppose the photon is absorbed. After the photon is absorbed, the electron's kinetic energy increases, which means the electron has to be in motion. However, where does the momentum come from? The electron can only change its momentum if there is an external force acting on it. There is no external force. Therefore, a free electron can’t simply swallow any photon and gain any of the photon's momentum. Even though the energy of a photon and an electron can change, they can do so only in compliance with established and unassailable physical laws. If we want to resolve the problem, we have to go back and consider the interaction with the atom, or rather an electron bound to an atom, for the atom can readily absorb the photon, transferring its energy to the electron. This is because the atom, unlike a free electron, has a large mass, and the atom as a whole can acquire the photon’s momentum without violating the laws of conservation. As a result, the electron can then gain the exact amount of energy and momentum.

**Question for a physicist: ** How are stars born according to the general theory of relativity? That's a fascinating question — thank you for asking! From the standpoint of general relativity (GR), stars are born, quite simply, from the gravitational collapse of large clouds of gas and dust. However, it is not quite as elementary as the above statement may imply, as the physics of star formation involves numerous factors that are not central to GR, but which still play a crucial role. Let me clarify and elaborate: The gas and dust that make up these clouds are primarily hydrogen and helium, with trace amounts of heavier elements. The gas is generally cold, with the temperature being in the range of tens of Kelvins or even less, but the gas clouds themselves are incredibly massive, consisting of millions or even billions of times the mass of our sun ("solar masses"). The gas clouds are not static; they are in constant motion, driven by turbulence, magnetic fields, and the internal pressure of the gas itself. Given their massive scale, they are not stable, and any small perturbation can initiate their collapse under gravitational forces. As the cloud contracts, the gravitational potential energy is converted into kinetic energy; the gas particles begin to collide more frequently and with increasing violence, leading to an increase in the temperature of the gas. This is akin to a car crash involving a huge pile of debris. The collapse is not uniform; different regions of the cloud contract at different rates, and fragments can break off to form individual stars or binary stars, which is to say, a pair of stars orbiting one another, linked by gravity. During the initial stages of collapse, the cloud is transparent to infrared radiation, which is essentially heat. As a result, most of the heat generated by the collapse can escape, and the collapse can proceed uninhibited. However, as it gets denser, the cloud becomes opaque, and the heat gets trapped. The increasing heat eventually halts the collapse, leading to a protostar. After the protostar forms, it continues to accumulate mass from the surrounding cloud, feeding matter, and becoming ever more dense, and ever hotter. Eventually, the core of the protostar reaches a sufficiently high temperature and density to initiate nuclear fusion. This is the moment the star "turns on;" a massive outflow of heat and light begins, signaling a new star has been born. The energy released by nuclear fusion creates an outward pressure that counterbalances the inward force of gravity. With the gravitational collapse stopped, the star enters a stable phase, steadily consuming its nuclear fuel.

Is it fair to say that there is the equivalent of infinite acceleration at the event horizon of a black hole? The answer is: No, it is not. You can be forgiven for thinking that it is because the gravitational field at the event horizon gets incredibly strong, and that the closer one gets to the event horizon, the stronger the gravitational field. But infinite acceleration? No. Let me explain. First, acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; and velocity itself is the rate of change of position. To calculate acceleration, we measure how an object’s speed is changing with respect to time. In a gravitational field, the change in velocity is the same for all objects, regardless of their mass or composition. If an object crosses the event horizon, the gravitational field at that point would be strongest, but the rate of change in velocity is not infinite, although, for an outside observer, it may appear that the rate is nearly infinite because of the effects of time dilation. An outside observer would never see an object cross the event horizon, the object seemingly freezes in time, and it approaches the event horizon asymptotically, but the object experiences its own clock ticking "normally". The object experiences a large, but finite acceleration. Also, one must consider that, the gravitational field is far greater than the acceleration needed to keep an object from the earth's surface.

If all of the mass energy of colliding black holes is contained within their event horizons, how does the collision release any energy? Stuff can escape from the event horizon if it collides with another? The short and simple answer is yes, the collision of two black holes releases energy, and the same mechanism that allows the release of energy also confines that energy within the event horizon of the final, merged black hole. Allow me to elaborate. The defining property of a black hole is the event horizon, a boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. However, black holes do not exist in isolation. They can collide. So, if two black holes collide, the final result will be a single black hole, more massive than either of the initial two, and therefore its event horizon will be also larger. If the total mass of the final black hole is less than the total mass of the two initial ones, then the difference must be radiated away as energy: In fact, a significant amount of energy, perhaps more than a few percent of the combined mass of the two black holes, can be radiated away, mostly in the form of gravitational waves. But where do the gravitational waves originate? From the event horizon, of course. They consist of fluctuations in the surrounding spacetime. And just as with light, they cannot escape the event horizon without a sufficient outward velocity; thus the energy is contained. But what if stuff collides with other stuff? If you send a high-energy particle into a black hole, it will eventually collide with all and everything that is inside it, and the collision would result in more particles. These newly materialized particles will, in turn, collide with other material particles, producing yet more particles, in a feedback cycle that eventually fills the event horizon. At the very least, the process should be governed by the same equations of general relativity, which do not allow for the escape of anything from within those event horizons... and it does not.

How do quarks give rise to the mass of protons and neutrons? This is a very good question. Let me attempt to give a brief explanation. The short answer is that quarks do not “give rise to” the mass of protons and neutrons. Neither do gluons. Most of the mass of the proton and neutron is due to the energy stored in the gluonic field. The Standard Model of particle physics treats quarks and gluons as fundamental point-like particles. Gluons are the mediators of the strong force that, in turn, binds the quarks together to form the nucleons (protons and neutrons.) Quarks and gluons, by themselves, have only a very small mass, but a lot of energy exists within the strong force field, the "glue" that holds them together. The quarks and gluons move around at close to the speed of light inside the nucleons, so, the mass of the proton or neutron is mostly the mass equivalent of this internal kinetic and potential energy of the quarks and gluons. Think of a spring. The mass of the spring (the metal itself) is only a tiny part of the mass of the system: most of the mass is the mass-equivalent of the potential energy stored in the stretched (or compressed) spring. In the case of a nucleon, the "spring" is the strong force field, and the "mass" is the mass-equivalent of the energy in that field. The Higgs field, which is also a quantum field, is responsible for the nonzero masses, albeit tiny, of fundamental particles like electrons or quarks. In this picture, the Higgs field is the "stuff" that interacts with other fundamental particles, giving rise to the (tiny) mass. The interaction, however, is weak and doesn’t make up the bulk of the mass of the proton and neutron: this is due to the strong force. So, when it comes to the mass of the proton, approximately one percent comes from the quarks, one percent comes from their kinetic energy, and the remaining 98 percent comes from the energy stored in the gluonic field.

If the “one-way” speed of light hasn’t yet been measured and we can just affirm the average 2-way speed of light for all points & perspectives is what measures c, what does that mean for ancient nighttime stars we see, that light’s not from long ago? That's a fascinating question, and the answer is multifaceted, touching upon fundamental aspects of relativity and observation. Let me elucidate. The fact that we can only directly measure the *two-way* speed of light, or that we *define* it to be constant in all directions, does indeed raise a subtle point when considering distant objects such as stars. Light from these stars does, without question, take a long time to reach us. The light we see tonight might have embarked on its journey millions, even billions, of years ago with our understanding of the universe's expansion included. Due to the immense distances, there is no practical way to measure the “one-way” speed, and even if we could, the concept might introduce complexities that are best avoided for now with respect to the precision of most calculations. To state it plainly: despite only measuring the two-way speed, the implications about the travel time of starlight remain essentially the same. The standard model of cosmology and our observations of the universe, including the observed redshift of distant galaxies and the cosmic microwave background, are exceedingly well-tested. They align with the idea that the expansion of the universe does affect the light traveling across vast distances. Consequently, even if the one-way speed of light were shown to be, in some sense, direction-dependent (which is not what our current experiments suggest), it wouldn’t invalidate the underlying principles that support our understanding of the universe. Furthermore, any hypothetical variation in the one-way speed of light would have to be exceedingly small, to the level of virtually undetectable, to be compatible with our existing astronomical and physical observations. Such a minute difference would likely manifest in subtle deviations from the expected behavior of the objects that emit or that the light illuminates, but these have yet to appear in real observations. Therefore, while the question is valid, the implications, in practical terms, tend to be minimal, and we can safely proceed with the assumption that the light that illuminates the cosmos, came, and continues to come, from events that, at that point in their proper time, took a very long time to reach us indeed.

A system composed by a piece of iron and a magnet has more energy if the iron is closer the magnet. So, the overall weight should be (very very slightly) different. Is there an intuitive thought experiment to show it? While I understand the question, I must state at the outset that the effect you ask about, if it exists, is almost certainly too minute to be measured in a thought experiment. However, let us proceed. The key to an intuitive thought experiment lies in the recognition that all forms of energy have an equivalent mass. A simple setup could involve two identical iron bars, each suspended from a very sensitive scale. Above one of the bars, we place a strong permanent magnet. Above the other, we place a non-magnetic metal bar. We then proceed to carefully measure the weight indicated by both scales. At the end of the experiment, the scale with the magnet has to be carefully calibrated and the magnetic force has to be taken into account, also. And yes, this calibration needs to be done prior to taking measurements. Now, let's imagine that the scale gives a slightly different indication or values. If the bar with the magnet pulls down with a slightly greater force, this indicates a larger quantity of energy in the combined system. This difference in weight is due to the stored potential energy in the magnetic field. Because the magnetic field is a form of energy, it will contribute to the overall mass-energy of the system. The closer the iron bar is to the magnet, the stronger the magnetic field, and thus, the greater the potential energy stored within that field. But the force of the magnet will be also pulling down and the scale will be affected. It's important to separate this from the effect we try to measure with the initial placement or positioning.  However, in reality, performing such an experiment and getting meaningful results is, for all practical purposes, impossible. The change in weight would be so infinitesimal that it is undetectable. It is, as I said, more of a thought experiment. If you can "observe" the effect, it implies a measurement technique sensitive enough to detect minute changes - which would be a genuine breakthrough.

Brian Greene said: “as particles … try to move through space, they have to burrow through the Higgs field, and that is what gives them mass”. Does that mean that particles that keep at rest in the frame of the Higgs fied are gravitationally massless? No. It does not. I presume that we are talking about the Higgs field and not just “the Higgs field”. The Higgs field permeates all of space. The Higgs field is a quantum field that has a non-zero value everywhere, even in regions where other quantum fields (e.g., electromagnetic fields) are zero. And although it is true that the Standard Model of particle physics (including the Higgs field) describes particles as “massless” when the Higgs field is turned off, that is a mathematical convenience that allows for simpler calculations, and it has nothing to do with the physics of the real world. The Higgs field is “always on”, so to speak. The Standard Model is also incomplete, and a “particle at rest” is only a matter of perspective. The Higgs field is not a fixed, immutable entity, but a quantum mechanical system. The value of the Higgs field at any given point varies and fluctuates. And yes, particles do interact with the Higgs field. That interaction is what gives the particles their mass. The word “massless” is, in this context, a misnomer because it creates a misleading image: as it refers not to the absence of mass but only to the absence of a mass term in the relevant equations. As the particles interact with the Higgs field, they acquire mass, and this mass is felt as gravitation. Particles that keep at rest in the frame of the Higgs field, therefore, still have mass: otherwise, they could not experience gravity. And now to explain why the Higgs field is so important in our physical reality, there is still another aspect that one should remember: the Higgs field is the only known field in the Standard Model that is thought to have a non-zero vacuum expectation value. This means that the Higgs field has a non-zero average value in the absence of any other particles or fields. This non-zero vacuum expectation value is what gives mass to all the other particles in the Standard Model. Without the Higgs field, the other particles would be massless, and the universe as we know it would not exist.

How does a black hole destroy matter but not light? Light is not "matter." Matter has mass, and an electromagnetic field, which is what constitutes light, has no mass. As a consequence, light will follow the same path as everything else. Now, it so happens that in the case of a black hole, the gravitational field is so intense that even light cannot escape. If the black hole is not rotating, the "escape velocity" is equal to the square root of 2GM/r, where G is Newton's gravitational constant, M is the mass of the black hole, and r is the distance from its center. The radius at which the escape velocity equals the speed of light is called the Schwarzschild radius, and as I mentioned, it is the boundary across which nothing, not even light, can escape. The Schwarzschild radius, in turn, is proportional to the mass of the black hole; for a black hole of one solar mass, it is about 3 kilometers. For a black hole of a million solar masses like those you find in galactic centers, it is 3 million kilometers. For the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, that number is approximately 12 million kilometers. A black hole "destroys" regular matter in that anything that falls across its event horizon is no longer part of the observable universe. It is not "destroyed" in the manner you might think: it is just no longer accessible. But it continues to exist. The mass remains, the electric charge remains, and the angular momentum remains. And, according to current theory, information remains as well. Now, you might have heard about "Hawking radiation," which posits a very slow loss of mass from a black hole. But this is a quantum mechanical effect that is separate from the usual processes that classical physics may be used to describe.

How is the speed of gravity determined? The speed of gravity is determined by observations of gravitational phenomena, and by the consistency of our physics models. In General Relativity, it is assumed to be the speed of light. This might seem somewhat counterintuitive, as gravity is a force, and not the propagation of anything. However, the “force” we call gravity is a manifestation of the curvature of spacetime, and the changes of this curvature, such as those caused by the motion of celestial objects, propagate. These changes, or "ripples," move at a finite speed: the speed of light in vacuum, the speed at which electromagnetic radiation, and also gravitational waves, propagate through the cosmos. This is not a philosophical assumption but a testable prediction. The experimental determination of the speed of gravity is very difficult, because the effects are so small and because the expected value is so high: a direct measurement would require equipment able to measure the time delay of propagating gravitational fields, which are very, very weak at large distances. However, we have observed them indirectly through the study of binary pulsars; these systems consist of a neutron star (a very dense star) and a white dwarf or another neutron star, orbiting one another. And we noticed that the orbit of these pairs is steadily shrinking. The rate of shrinkage is precisely consistent with the predictions of General Relativity — which, in turn, require the speed of gravity to be the speed of light — and inconsistent with any alternative with a smaller value of the speed of gravity. Furthermore, in 2017, the collaborative effort LIGO and Virgo directly observed gravitational waves generated by the merger of two neutron stars. The detection was followed by the observation of an associated gamma-ray burst and a related optical signal emitted at different wavelengths. The time delay between the waves detected via the different methods matched perfectly the prediction: that is, the speed of gravity matches the speed of light.

How can virtual particles become real particles e.g. while Hawking radiation? This is a very fundamental question. Virtual particles are mathematical constructs, or, if you prefer, artifacts of calculations. They are not “real” in the sense that they cannot be detected directly. Virtual particles that appear in calculations are the building blocks of interactions, specifically, of force-carrying fields. Take, for instance, the exchange of virtual photons between two electrons. This is, at its mathematical core, the mechanism by which electrons exert their electrostatic force on one another. But the virtual photon’s existence is only temporary. It disappears as it propagates, and the electromagnetic field itself remains undisturbed. Nonetheless, the equations of quantum field theory tell us that the virtual photon carries energy, momentum, and (most important for this discussion) mass. The key here is the uncertainty principle, and the concept of “virtual.” Energy conservation can be violated – but only by a small amount, and only for a short period of time. A virtual particle appears, it exists, and, in the vacuum of the field, it immediately disappears. Now imagine a black hole. Its gravity is so strong that spacetime itself is distorted. The vacuum is no longer empty. Energy is abundant, curvature is immense, and all of the simple rules are broken. Pair production can and does occur, meaning, a virtual particle (e.g., a virtual electron-positron pair) can now become a real particle where “real” means here, that the created particle travels to infinity, forever! One of the particles in the pair might fall into the black hole, while the other, if it escapes, is observed as Hawking radiation. The Hawking radiation represents the black hole emitting energy, and, consequently, losing mass. This is the mechanism by which black holes “evaporate” over immense timescales.

I’m having a bit of trouble understanding how to visualize elementary particles as waves but doing the photon/gluon/virtual particle interaction processes. I do not understand why antimatter is visually necessary in field animations. Why? The issue stems from a fundamental misunderstanding of what these animations depict. They're not meant to be literal representations of reality; that is, they're not depicting "photons" or "gluons" as actual particles. Instead, these are diagrams that are meant to allow us a view of how to calculate a quantum-mechanical probability amplitude. Quantum field theory, and indeed quantum mechanics in general, deals with a certain class of calculations. This class of calculations uses quantities that (a) can be measured and that (b) evolve in space and time. The field animations you describe are essentially cartoons about how these quantities interact with one another, as a visual aid. Keep in mind that these calculations don't "know" of any such things as "time", or "space". The theory deals with operators, states, and their evolution. To then apply the results of that calculation to what we see, we have to interpret these calculations. In this interpretation, we say things like, “a particle did this” or “a force carrier did that.” Now, to your specific questions. In a classical-mechanical world, you could use a mathematical method to calculate how a ball will interact with a wall... say, billiard balls. If you have a good enough mathematical model and access to the initial state of the system, you can predict everything. In quantum field theory, the underlying equations do not deal with trajectories, only the evolution of states. So, the initial state we want to describe is the “incoming particles”. Likewise, to build the model, we take mathematical expressions to describe the "interaction" of those particles. And, of course, we need to determine the "outgoing particles" after the interaction. The intermediate states are not directly observed. The idea of a "virtual particle" is nothing more than a shorthand term for what is happening here.  The mathematical expressions used involve mathematical objects such as complex numbers or linear operators. We create and add up probabilities (amplitudes, to be more specific) associated with every possible route from the initial to the final states. This is where the diagrams come in. These diagrams, often referred to as Feynman diagrams, are useful because they provide a visual shorthand for this calculation and they enable us to avoid getting lost in the mathematical weeds. Such diagrams are very useful because you can, at a glance, understand what calculations need to be done.  As to your question about why antimatter makes an appearance in these field animations: Antimatter is not "visually necessary" in the animation to the extent that it is literally physically present. The key word here is "quantum mechanics" and we have to remember that quantum mechanics is described by operators satisfying specific commutation relationships. In quantum mechanical systems you need to use the mathematical "trick" of introducing and eliminating particles that are not observed, in order to perform a specific calculation. These virtual particles, as they are called, are often paired with their antiparticles to cancel certain mathematical features of the calculation. The net result, upon interpretation, is a specific type of interaction. Without those intermediate steps, the appropriate results simply don't follow. The reason it looks like the interaction involves matter and antimatter is because a particle and its antiparticle have opposite electric charge. In a Feynman diagram, we assign a direction to the lines and interpret it as either a particle (traveling forward in time) or an antiparticle (traveling backward in time). This is, of course, just a shorthand, a visual trick. It is a consequence of the structure of the underlying quantum mechanical equations: The equations themselves do not care about any concept of direction of time or charge.

According to relativity, gravity slows time (time dilation) and causes length contraction? Does Dark Energy, which is accelerating the expansion of the Universe, speed time and cause lengthening is space? You are correct in the premise of your first question. Time does slow down in a gravitational field, and lengths contract along the direction in which the gradient of the gravitational field is the strongest. As for Dark Energy, however, the answer is much trickier. First, we must define what we mean by “speed up time” or “cause lengthening.” In general relativity, we measure time with clocks and lengths with rulers. Thus, “speeding up time” means that a clock ticks faster. And, “causing lengthening” means that the distance between two points increases. Dark Energy accelerates the expansion of spacetime. What this means is that distances between gravitationally unbound objects increase. But we do not notice this within gravitationally bound systems. For example, the Earth is getting farther and farther from the Sun due to Dark Energy, but only at a rate of micrometers per year. But the distances between the Earth and the Moon, or between you and me, are not significantly affected. So, Dark Energy’s effect on time is that it causes the rate of expansion of the universe to accelerate. This, in itself, is not a direct “speeding up of time” in a given local region, because it is the *rate of change of the expansion* that is affected. As a result of the accelerated expansion, the rate at which objects recede from one another increases. This is the effect of Dark Energy that is most immediately measurable. Moreover, Dark Energy’s influence on the local rate of time is, by any realistic measure, negligible.

How is mass not conserved when it's literally E^2-p^2, and both quantities are conserved? This is a valid question, and an excellent one, too. To begin with, energy and (linear) momentum are indeed conserved. This is a fundamental property that is independent of the mass of a particle. This means that the total energy and the total momentum of a closed system remain constant over time. The equation you mention, E² - p² = m², is a fundamental identity in relativistic physics, linking energy (E), momentum (p), and mass (m). Note that I am using natural units throughout, where the speed of light c=1 which is the standard in theoretical physics. In these units, energy and momentum have the same dimension and mass has the same dimension; and mass is conserved. However, what you may have in mind is that the *mass* of a system does not equal the *sum* of the masses of the components.  Here's why: consider a system of two protons at rest in a box. The protons each have a mass m, and they are at rest. The total energy of the system is thus 2m, and the total momentum zero. Now, imagine they collide and stick together. The mass of the final particle, which we will call a diproton, must be calculated to be a factor of √2 smaller than twice that of the proton. Yes, the mass has diminished. But the total mass of the system need not be the sum of the masses of its component parts. After the collision, thermal energy is radiated away, and the remaining energy and momentum of the diproton are sufficient for the overall system to obey conservation of energy and momentum, as required by the laws of physics. This is because the mass of a particle or system actually represents its *rest energy*, and energy itself is conserved. A similar idea applies to things like atomic nuclei, which have a total mass measurably less than the sum of their protons and neutrons. The difference is the so-called *binding energy*, which is the energy required to separate the component parts of a system.  Now, it is time to talk about mass and energy in general relativity. Remember that in general relativity, gravity is treated as a curvature of spacetime. So the presence of energy and momentum (represented in the stress-energy tensor, to be precise) causes this curvature. It is not a stretch to say that energy *is* gravity. This means that the *mass* of a system is not a constant. Instead, the mass of the system is equivalent to the *energy* of the system, and energy is conserved. As the system evolves, and even when components are exchanged, the energy remains the same. Thus, in general relativity, the mass-energy equivalence is a direct manifestation of the conservation of energy. Consider the case of a black hole, which is a region of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. The mass of a black hole is equivalent to the energy needed to form it, and this energy is not conserved, as the system is constantly radiating energy in the form of Hawking radiation, which decreases its mass over time.

Is there empirical evidence against John Moffat's modified gravity (MOG), also known as Scalar-Tensor-Vector-Gravity (STVG)? I am inclined to say no, but I concede that it is not quite that simple. The primary reason I say "no" is because Moffat's theory, while elegant, has never managed to make accurate predictions, especially at the scales where it should, in principle, outperform the standard model. As a reminder, MOG was developed to explain the observed rotation curves of spiral galaxies without invoking dark matter, or, at least, without requiring as much as the standard model does. Essentially, the theory introduces a spatially varying gravitational constant, as well as two additional vector and scalar fields, to reproduce the effects of dark matter. This, in itself, is not necessarily a problem; after all, the standard model of particle physics has many adjustable parameters whose values are, in a sense, arbitrary. But those parameters are nonetheless precisely defined. MOG, in contrast, is not terribly predictive. The parameters are not completely arbitrary, but they are flexible enough to allow the theory to match the observed rotation curves… and that is just the problem. It fits, it does explain; however, one can always find other models — and indeed, other explanations — that fit just as well. Even more critically, MOG has failed to account for several other observations that the standard model readily explains, and even predicts. I will give you a couple of examples out of many. The existence of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) is readily explained in the standard model, and so are the measurements of its very slight temperature variations across the sky. MOG, however, has never been able to convincingly account for those variations. Or consider the distribution of galaxies across the sky. That, too, is accounted for by the standard model, which predicts the existence of a large-scale structure that indeed matches observations. MOG, however, has never managed to predict the correct large-scale structure. Lastly, there is the matter of gravitational lensing by galaxy clusters. The standard model accurately accounts for the observed lensing effect. MOG, on the other hand, has had difficulty in this area. If one is generous, one can try to tweak the theory and make it consistent with observations… but that involves inserting additional parameters, further eroding the theory's predictive power. So, to reiterate: there is not a single observation that definitively rules out MOG, for one can always make the theory match observations by adjusting its parameters. But there are numerous observations that MOG struggles with; observations that standard model handles with relative ease. And that to me, and to most physicists in general, is rather damning.

Is it true that everything travels at a constant velocity in deep space, near the speed of light? No, it is not. The speed of light is constant, and the speed of light is an important constant. Particles with no rest mass, such as photons, travel at the speed of light, always and everywhere. However, objects with mass cannot. Einstein's special theory of relativity tells us that mass increases as velocity increases. Therefore, a massive object can only approach the speed of light asymptotically, i.e., it can get arbitrarily close, but can never, ever reach the speed of light. Even the tiniest mass will slow down an object from reaching such speed. This has nothing to do with space, deep or otherwise, it is a fundamental property. Now, regarding velocity, anything devoid of external forces will travel at constant velocity, following Newton's first law of motion. It is possible, of course, to avoid all external forces in deep space. You have to stay far away from stars, black holes, and galaxies, and you must resist the solar wind, the cosmic microwave background radiation, to name a few. But if you do, yes, anything will travel in a straight line at a constant velocity. Keep in mind, however, that the Universe is expanding, and the expansion is accelerating, and therefore even in deep space, you will be affected by this universal acceleration. In the end, the statement that everything travels at some constant velocity in deep space is only partially correct: massive objects can only approach the speed of light, but they can also travel at any other speed as long as no external forces are applied, with an important caveat (the expansion of the universe).

Isn’t it true that the general theory of relativity suggests the existence of black holes, white holes, negative value e=mc2 energy, wormholes, quantum entanglement, cosmological, constant gravitational waves, and a host of other amazing things? Yes, that is indeed true. The general theory of relativity, or GR for short, is a truly remarkable achievement, perhaps the most successful scientific theory of all time, and it does indeed suggest all of those things. Black holes are, in fact, the first to have been predicted rigorously by GR itself; white holes, I wouldn’t say so: they are a theoretical construct, a solution to the equations of GR, so they can exist, in the mathematical sense, but not as a consequence of the theory. As for negative energy values, yes, sometimes we run into these. The most dramatic example is perhaps in the Casimir effect where space-time fluctuations give rise to something that effectively acts as negative energy. Wormholes? Again a theoretical construct, and not one I’d put much stock in. Quantum entanglement is a feature of quantum mechanics, and it is perfectly compatible with GR, though the two theories have yet to be reconciled completely. Cosmological constants: yes, they are needed to explain the observed accelerated expansion of the universe. Gravitational waves, also predicted by GR, and detected for the first time some years ago, confirming Einstein’s theory. In summary, GR is an incredibly vast and rich theory, with far-reaching implications.
