But it's important to bear in mind that while the predictions of GR are frequently amazing, some of these predictions remain theoretical, still debated, and not all are necessarily true.

How can Victor K. Toth say that matter does not create gravity, when the Nobel Prize winning physicist, Stephen Weinberg said that it’s a two-way street, “matter creates space-time, and space-time determines matter’s path”? My name is Viktor Toth, and I would like to clarify my previous statement and to address this question. The idea that “matter creates space-time” can be misleading, but it certainly does not invalidate any part of Einstein’s theory of General Relativity. The relationship between matter and gravity is intricate, and the language one uses to describe it is especially important. What Weinberg meant, as a shorthand, is that matter is the source of the gravitational field, and the gravitational field, in turn, affects its path, like the famous curve that light follows near a massive celestial body. It is a “two-way street” in the sense that they influence each other. However, it is critically important to use the correct words for the relationship. Matter (or more precisely, energy-momentum) is the *source* of the gravitational field. That field describes how spacetime is curved and how things move. This is what the field equations of General Relativity are all about. I would, however, emphasize that space-time itself does *not* create the gravitational field, which is a physical field that is present even in empty space and carries energy and momentum, like the electromagnetic field. Now, the gravitational field, in turn, determines the motion of matter, including light. It's like this: You put a mass somewhere, and it creates a gravitational field. The gravitational field determines how other matter will move, including other masses or light itself, and that is the essence of the "two-way street". However, it is the gravitational field that mediates that interaction, not space-time. To reiterate and clarify: Matter does not “create” gravity or time itself, *contrary to what some may say*. It creates a gravitational *field*, a physical entity which, in turn, affects spacetime. This field is what “tells” matter how to move. Weinberg was, of course, one of the most brilliant physicists of his generation, I would encourage anyone to read his words carefully, to understand the very subtle meanings behind them.

What is the cause of a black hole's immense strength? How is it possible for something to have infinite density and gravity? A “massive” gravitational pull is not the same thing as immense strength. The gravitational pull of a black hole is only immensely strong near the black hole, because (and only because) it is extremely compact. Infinite density? Infinite gravity? Well, let me put it this way… We call a black hole “singular” because general relativity, and indeed all of physics we know, breaks down at the center of a black hole. Near the center, there needs to be something “special”, a breakdown of the conventional laws of physics, a singularity. What this actually means is that we don’t know. We don’t know what happens in that small area of space, and we’re unlikely to know anytime soon. What we do know is that, far enough away from the singularity, a black hole’s gravity (and its mass) can be described quite accurately using general relativity. This, in turn, is just a theory based on the concept of spacetime curvature. But again, please do remember that general relativity, though experimentally tested in a variety of different ways, is nonetheless just a theory: a useful, powerful one, certainly…but the final word? Far from it. Singularities, infinite density, and infinite gravity are, from the standpoint of our current understanding, a breakdown of that theory, nothing more. Also, be mindful of this: No experiment we are capable of performing can either prove or disprove “infinite density” or “infinite gravity.” And it isn’t necessarily a physical property: it is merely a calculation.

Why is graviton difficult to detect? Do we have any good reasons to believe it exits in the first place? Gravitons, as far as we know, if they exist at all, are exceedingly weakly interacting particles. This is a consequence of their supposed spin-2 nature and the fact that gravity is an extremely weak force. Consider the following seemingly obvious fact: we are constantly bombarded by electromagnetic radiation. Light, to be precise, and its intensity is measurable, not negligible. A single photon carries momentum; it can be scattered from matter, and this is something we can measure, and we can put a number on it. But we are not constantly bombarded by gravitational radiation. Gravitational waves, in contrast to electromagnetic waves, are so weak that we only rarely observe them. When we do, it is because something really massive is involved: merging black holes is the canonical example. We infer their existence indirectly from the fact that we have excellent theoretical reasons to believe in them. Gravity is modeled as a field, and we know by decades of experimental evidence that other fundamental forces, like electromagnetism, have corresponding fundamental particles, photons, as quantum excitations of their respective fields. Granted, the gravitational field, unlike the electromagnetic field, is related to spacetime geometry, but general relativity, our best theory of gravity, is a classical theory. It needs to be quantized, just like the electromagnetic field. Since the force carriers of the electromagnetic field are photons, it is a reasonable assumption that the quantum excitations of the gravitational field, whatever that may be, should be a yet-to-be-discovered particle, and hence, the graviton. The graviton, if it exists, also presents significant challenges to detection. Gravity is a very weak force. Consider the amount of matter that is needed to produce a detectable gravitational wave. To put it differently, for any process to create a gravitational wave, it must involve a huge mass with extremely high acceleration. It’s a double whammy: not only is gravity weak, but we need a very massive system undergoing enormous acceleration to produce a detectable signal. The only known processes that can do this involve either neutron stars (which are difficult to study because they are very far away) or black holes (which are even more intractable, by definition). It’s a daunting prospect, indeed.

What are the challenges and potential designs for a SpaceX Interstellar probe using miniaturized black hole propulsion, theorized to harness Hawking radiation as thrust? The short answer is that, as far as I know, the concept of a SpaceX Interstellar probe employing miniaturized black hole propulsion and the harnessing of Hawking radiation as thrust, is pure science fiction, far beyond currently conceivable technology. Let me elaborate. First, we’d need to be able to generate and/or capture a microscopic black hole. Now, some people believe that it might be possible to generate small black holes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The issue is, we have not done so, and even if we did, the lifetime of such a microscopic black hole would be incredibly short indeed. Next, we’d need to develop miniaturized propulsion systems. I’m not sure if such a thing exists. However, for the sake of argument, let’s assume that the process would be something like this: the black hole would theoretically emit Hawking radiation, which could be directed to provide thrust. It would, in essence, be a miniature, exceedingly inefficient, rocket engine. Another challenge is that the amount of radiation would be tiny, making for incredibly low thrust, and even if the amount of radiation and thrust are enough, it would require a lot of energy to maintain (capture, create and/or find) the black hole. The energy needs would likely outweigh the benefits, but let’s suppose we figure out how to overcome all of the above challenges, and we are now able to build this interstellar probe. Where do we get the black hole? As you already know, we are no longer talking about something that is merely difficult. The black hole would need to be captured or created from scratch with immense energy. It would need to be safely contained, and controlled with unprecedented precision. The next challenge would be the fact that the probe would be constantly losing mass as the black hole evaporates due to Hawking radiation, which would change its mass, size, and thrust constantly. The probe’s trajectory would be highly erratic and difficult to control. Given all the above considerations, this design would prove to be exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, with our current level of technology.

Do electromagnetic waves have momentum? If so, do waves and sound waves have momentum? Yes, electromagnetic waves do have momentum. Because they have energy, and, due to the equivalence of mass and energy, momentum is an inevitable consequence. Sound waves, on the other hand, do carry momentum, but it is a slightly different story. Sound waves are not a fundamental field, like the electromagnetic field – they are, instead, a disturbance that propagates through a medium. Because of that, sound waves do not have their own individual intrinsic energy or momentum. The same holds true for other types of mechanical waves, such as water waves or seismic waves. The energy and momentum associated with those waves are the energy and momentum *of the medium itself*, being carried by the wave. When a sound wave propagates through the air, it causes the air molecules to move. Therefore the wave transports energy and momentum, but ultimately, the momentum is the momentum of those molecules. It is important to note that even though sound waves or water waves do carry momentum, the amount of momentum they carry is usually negligible. The momentum of an individual electromagnetic wave, in contrast, can be quite significant. Think, for example, of an atom emitting a photon: the atom recoils as a result of conservation of momentum. The photon carries away all the momentum. The same applies to a charged particle being accelerated by an electromagnetic field. Momentum, which is an attribute of almost all forms of energy, helps us understand how all these phenomena relate to each other.

What is the origin of the energy resulting in an explosion during the merger of two neutron stars that do not result in a black hole? The origin of the energy lies in the conversion of gravitational potential energy into thermal energy. Neutron stars, being extremely compact objects with immense gravity, possess a tremendous amount of gravitational potential energy. As two neutron stars spiral toward each other, their mutual gravitational attraction accelerates them to incredibly high speeds, close to the speed of light in the final moments before the merger. This acceleration is such that the kinetic energy of the system increases dramatically. When the stars collide, virtually all of this kinetic energy is instantly converted into thermal energy. The process takes a tiny fraction of a second, yet the energy released is enormous. If a black hole does not form, a remnant neutron star will exist and much of this energy is also released as kinetic energy in the form of ejected matter as well as electromagnetic radiation. This energy can also be released in the form of gravitational waves, which is the "ripples" in spacetime predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity. One should also remember that in neutron stars, the strong nuclear force competes directly with gravity, trying to push the star apart while gravity tries to collapse it. The equation of state for nuclear matter at such extreme densities is not precisely known. It is the subject of intense research, both theoretical and experimental, and a lot of the energy released stems from the rearrangement of the nuclear matter, and the resultant release of particles.
