What has prevented Europe to stay unified like China since the collapse of Rome given they have far less people to govern than China? Europe has always been a patchwork, and I suppose that is its defining character. I am not an historian, but it is my understanding the Roman Empire was, essentially, a single political entity, with the exception being its brief division which wasn't as disruptive as it may appear at a glance. The Chinese dynasties went through periods of disunity too, but the crucial difference is after the fact: they always reunified. Why Europe failed to follow suit is, no doubt, a complicated question, but I can offer a few thoughts. One, there were always more competing powers in Europe. The geography itself is fragmented, with many mountain ranges and bodies of water dividing the landscape; China, on the other hand, has massive rivers, vast plains, and natural routes of communication. Two, Europe had the pesky, and not to be dismissed, presence of the Catholic Church, a powerful and centralized institution that vied for power with the secular governments. In China, emperors had always retained control of spiritual matters. Three, there has always been a remarkable degree of ethnic and linguistic diversity in Europe. China has always been comparatively homogenous, with a few notable exceptions. This meant fewer sources of friction within the empire. Four, there was the matter of the "barbarians," the tribes on the peripheries whom the Romans had to fight for centuries. They eventually contributed to the collapse of the Western Roman Empire. The resulting waves of migration and instability, or at least the lasting memory of those events contributed to lasting power vacuums. It's an intriguing subject, and I am certain that I am overlooking numerous critical factors, but I assume this will suffice until one of my readers can expand further on these considerations.

Is there any way, other than throwing some mass in the opposite direction, to move forward in space? Yes, there is. While throwing some mass in the opposite direction is a practical example, the underlying principle is conservation of momentum. In a closed system, the total momentum remains constant. So you can achieve propulsion even without expelling mass outside your body. Think of how a spider moves in zero gravity. It will not be able to expel mass. But the spider can spin a web and then pull on the web and it will move. Another example would be an astronaut working around a satellite, in order to grab a floating tool. She can hold the tool away from herself and then move her arms, and by moving them forward she can move her body back. When the tool is closer, the body moves less; when the tool is farther, the body moves more. Another example of this sort of "internal propulsion" involves the use of electromagnetic or gravitational fields. If you can change your position significantly enough to interact with these fields in a way that does not conserve momentum within your body, you will be be able to move. Lastly, I feel that there is a general misconception about space travel. Sure, it is hard. But we seem constantly to emphasize the "getting there" while completely ignoring that the hardest part is keeping the crew alive, in the often hostile conditions of the void. I have never seen a good explanation of how to feed and hydrate the crew, for example, on a multi-year voyage to another solar system, nor have I seen a discussion of shielding from cosmic radiation without massive quantities of lead, or the psychological effects of being cooped up for such a long period of time with a few other people who are complete strangers to them.

What if when your at the singularity of a black hole (if there is one), looking back out to space may look like a singularity also? Can that be? I am assuming by "singularity," you mean the point inside a black hole where current theoretical physics predicts an infinite density and curvature of spacetime. Now, if we define "looking back out to space" as observing the universe from a vantage point at or near this theoretical singularity, the answer, unfortunately, is that we cannot even begin to know. We can't even make the same measurement or observation twice, according to current theory. The problem is quite fundamental. General Relativity (the theory of gravitation) and Quantum Mechanics (the theory of the very small) are incompatible. The singularity is where gravity (General Relativity) becomes extraordinarily strong, and where we expect quantum effects to become important. At the singularity, all current theories break down. It is like trying to drive a car on a road that has suddenly evaporated. We have no tools to calculate what happens. But to venture a guess – what kind of guess would it be? To imagine a view from the singularity would require us to merge General Relativity and Quantum Mechanics into a single "Theory of Everything". And, by the definition of "singularity," what we could "see" or "observe" from that point would be altered by infinite values, by that extreme curvature of spacetime. So, in principle, your guess might be correct. But at this point, it's nothing more than a guess.

If a light ray of white light is bent by the gravity of a massive object like a star, does the light ray undergo diffraction and turn into a rainbow? No, the effect does not produce a rainbow. As described by General Relativity, light rays are deflected by gravity, but they do not undergo diffraction in the same way that, let's say, light rays passing through a prism do. The deflection, or "bending," is caused by the curvature of spacetime around a massive object, and so white light, each color with a different wavelength and frequency, does not diffract. Instead, each different wavelength of the light is affected in almost exactly the same fashion. The effect is such that instead of a rainbow, the light forms an arc around the object. This phenomenon is known as "gravitational lensing". When you look at a point source of light from behind a gravitational lens, you may see multiple images of that source, or if it's especially massive, this may even manifest as a ring. If, however, we were to entertain a hypothetical scenario where the light does indeed diffract because of the enormous gravity, then, yes, it could form a rainbow, although this is by no means based in reality. Yet, keep in mind that, even in this hypothetical situation, you would see a rainbow only with a source of white light or a source consisting of many different colors. If you had a source of monochromatic light, only a single band of color would result, with no diffraction. And finally, let me add a small warning: Do not confuse gravitational lensing with the "rainbow" that is sometimes observed in the atmosphere. These are indeed due to diffraction or refraction, or a combination of both, of sunlight through water droplets (rain and fog) or ice crystals(ice halos) in the atmosphere.

Is Newton's conception of gravity as incompatible with Einstein's concept of gravity, as Einstein's is from the quantum? How, or how not? The question poses a valid point, and I appreciate the opportunity to clarify. Let's begin with a straightforward "yes." Newton's and Einstein's concepts of gravity are, indeed, incompatible. It is not merely a matter of one being an improved version of the other––though that statement also holds––but fundamental differences arise when analyzing the core principles. Similarly, Einstein's theory of gravity, or general relativity, has deep-seated fundamental incompatibilities with quantum mechanics. Newton described and quantified gravity with reasonable accuracy, and predicted with astonishing precision. His equations work incredibly well, and they remain valid today for a vast range of situations. They do not, however, provide a complete description of gravity. Einstein, on the other hand, reinterpreted gravity as a manifestation of spacetime curvature. And this insight fundamentally changed the nature of the gravitational force itself: it is no longer a force, but a property of space-time. These concepts are not merely different, they are mathematically and conceptually distinct, and that's where the incompatibility lies. For instance, General Relativity accurately predicts phenomena Newton's theory cannot. As examples, it explains the precession of Mercury's orbit, and the deflection of starlight during solar eclipses which validated general relativity immediately after its conception. However, it becomes even more intricate when we introduce quantum mechanics. Quantum mechanics, for its part, describes the behavior of matter and energy at the atomic and subatomic levels. Attempts to reconcile general relativity and quantum mechanics, which many brilliant minds have pursued, encounter significant issues. One such issue is the very nature of the gravitational field. Quantum field theory treats forces as being mediated by particles, which fits the framework well. This approach leads to the concept of the "graviton". However, the math involved in this treatment quickly becomes intractable. The difficulties are so formidable that physicists have had to come up with novel concepts. The theory of loop quantum gravity and superstring theory, for instance, are potential candidates that attempt to bridge the divide between the two, offering alternative approaches to quantum gravity; but regardless, these are ongoing areas of active research, and definitive answers remain some time away.

Can anything emerge in space other than mass and energy to be equivalent and convertible to mass or energy? If it can then how will we write E=mc2? The question is subtly worded, almost philosophical in nature. The answer is perhaps a matter of definition. Let me rephrase the question, to ensure that I am aligned with the intent. The question is, essentially, can we have anything apart from mass and energy that has an equivalence to mass or energy and is subject to interchange with mass or energy? And if so, how does it interact with the most famous equation in all of physics? My answer is, yes, we absolutely can. How? Recall that E=mc² does not apply to mass alone but rather to mass-energy equivalence. The *E* in the formula stands for the total energy of a body, including all of its kinetic, potential, and internal energy. So, just as we can convert mass into energy and vice versa, so can *any* form of energy be converted into energy or mass.  Now, what are the things that can be interchanged with energy and mass, besides mass and energy? Well, consider the other conserved quantities, such as momentum or angular momentum. Both momentum and angular momentum can be readily exchanged with mass or energy. Furthermore, the exchange is dictated by the special theory of relativity. Again, consider a somewhat contrived, yet physically meaningful example: suppose that two identical particles of matter, each with mass *m*, approach one another at high speed, traveling in opposite directions. The total momentum of the system is, by definition, zero. The rest energy of the system is just 2*mc². Now envision them colliding, and the two particles annihilating, yielding two photons. The two photons, with zero rest mass. have a total energy of 2*mc², but also have zero momentum. Now, the laws of conservation of energy and momentum dictated both must be considered in this process. This is also why many physicists, when discussing the equation, often talk about "mass-energy equivalence". And, obviously, other conserved quantities play an important role in the interaction.

Why does general relativity predict that the wavelength of light will be shifted due to the galaxies mass in an effect called gravitational redshift? Not quite. The gravitational redshift is not a direct consequence of a galaxy's mass, but of any massive object. General relativity predicts that the wavelength of light emitted from or passing through a strong gravitational field will be stretched, meaning its frequency decreases and its wavelength increases, appearing redder; hence, "redshift". The effect is not specific to galaxies, though galaxies, being massive, exhibit this effect. The amount of redshift is proportional to the gravitational potential, that is, the strength of the gravitational field at the point of emission or observation. It arises because time slows down in a stronger gravitational field. As light travels out of a gravitational field, it has to "climb uphill," its frequency decreases, and its corresponding wavelength lengthens. Conversely, if the light travels into a deeper gravitational well, its frequency increases, and its wavelength shortens, a blueshift. This effect has been experimentally verified; one does not need a “galaxy” to observe this, the experiment can be performed in a laboratory. For example, the slight gravitational redshift of light emitted from the Earth's surface has been measured. The effect is more pronounced near extremely massive and compact objects like black holes, where the gravitational field is exceptionally strong. In the context of galaxies, it can be used as a probe to study the distribution of mass, including dark matter, within the galaxy itself; but this is only one application.

Why does the weakness of gravity prevent scientists from finding the graviton? The question, admittedly, is a bit backwards. The weakness of gravity does not "prevent" us from finding the graviton, any more than the weakness of, say, the electric charge of an electron prevents us from studying electromagnetism. The fact remains that the Standard Model of particle physics is a remarkable construction, but it does not include gravity, nor does it provide any clue on how to incorporate gravity. In the Standard Model, particle interactions are described by a gauge group, and these interactions are mediated by vector bosons, specifically the photon, the W and Z bosons, and the gluons. The graviton is a hypothetical particle which has not yet been observed, and there is much speculation, but no theory, on what properties it has or is supposed to have. Some theories suggest the graviton could be massless like the photon, some suggest it could be massive, and what's more, some of the hypothetical properties are inherently untestable, such as the suggestion that the graviton is a constituent of the "bulk" in extra spatial dimensions. There are also various approaches to a theory of quantum gravity, each with its own issues, such as quantum general relativity, string theory and loop quantum gravity. These theories, if and when they are fully developed, might offer a framework for the graviton, but as of today, this particle has not been directly observed or detected. In fact, a direct detection of the graviton seems exceedingly unlikely. And yes, gravity is the weakest force we know of. But that is hardly the main reason why the graviton has eluded detection to date. It could be that the graviton is, in fact, not a particle at all. It may well be that gravity cannot be described in terms of force-carrying particles. Or, it's possible that the graviton does exist, but it is simply not the right concept for a correct description of quantum gravity, the way we believe.

If we accept that dark matter exist, they must be part of the entire planet Earth, including living plant and animal organisms. In this case, is it correct to believe that dark matter is part of the human organism? Yes, if dark matter exists and permeates all “regular” matter, then it is indeed part of the human organism. The percentage is, of course, minuscule, much less than the amount of water or oxygen. Then again, we are also made of trace elements, such as gold, or uranium. Whether dark matter interacts with regular matter through the force of gravity and/or through some as-yet-undiscovered mechanism is an ongoing debate. If there is a new type of interaction, it is almost certainly extremely weak; otherwise, we would have already detected it one way or another. What is clear is that dark matter is definitely a form of matter. It has mass, and is therefore subject to gravity, so in that sense, it must be present with us, inside us, passing through us. It is also a type of matter that has never been directly observed, which leaves many questions unanswered. And the more we learn, the more questions they will ask. For instance, what is the distribution of dark matter throughout the human body? Does it mostly concentrate in the bones, or does muscle, or the brain, have a higher concentration? Does the concentration of dark matter in our body change over time? Does it obey the laws of thermodynamics? Does it have some kind of “temperature”? We don’t know. The universe is full of surprises, and the more we look, the stranger things become.

Was the German mathematician Hilbert's final derivation of the general relativity found to contain a key error by subsequent peer scholars? So Einstein is still regarded as the first person to publish the correct equations of general relativity? Yes, to the best of my knowledge. Hilbert, who was a brilliant mathematician, published his equations of general relativity shortly before Einstein published his, but Hilbert’s were, indeed, found to be flawed. The crucial mistake lay not in the mathematics itself, but in the boundary conditions he used. Einstein, whose equations were correct in every respect, is therefore credited with correctly formulating the theory of general relativity first. This is not to diminish Hilbert’s accomplishment in any way. His contributions to mathematics, including the formalization of Hilbert space, were foundational. Moreover, the fact that he was working on these equations at the same time as Einstein, and in fact published his results first, only underlines the revolutionary nature of the times and the rapid progress made in theoretical physics at the beginning of the 20th century. It is worth noting that some historians, however, have suggested that both men arrived at the equations independently and at roughly the same time. There is ongoing debate about whose work took precedence, but at the end of the day, it is Einstein who is given the nod. Perhaps, and this is just my personal view and opinion, it is because, as I understand the history of science, Einstein had a deeper understanding of the underlying *physics* and could interpret the mathematical solutions properly. Pure mathematics, while invaluable, only takes you so far. The physical intuition, based on years of working with problems in physics is just as crucial. In the end, the proof lies in the pudding: The equations are a reflection of how reality works.

What is the propagator for a massless scalar field, and how can you compute it using C++? The first part of the question is easy. The propagator for a massless scalar field, also sometimes called the Feynman propagator, is a Green’s function. Specifically, it is a solution to the wave equation, which is a partial differential equation. The second part is a bit more challenging. I am not a programmer; I am not particularly skilled in C++, and I certainly am not in the habit of writing code for others. Still, I can explain what would be involved, assuming you have (1) a good theoretical understanding of the wave equation, (2) a good understanding of numerical methods, and (3) a good understanding of C++. The first hurdle is that a Green’s function is a mathematical idealization: it has a singularity at the origin. In other words, it blows up as you approach the point (x, y, z, t) = (0, 0, 0, 0). You need to use a numerical approximation, and there are many ways to do it. You can use a finite-difference scheme, a finite-element method, or a spectral method; all have their pros and cons. Then you'll need to choose a spacetime discretization, choosing a grid size and time step (these need to be carefully chosen to ensure stability and convergence). Then you need to write your C++ code. I will caution you though that you must keep it in mind that the numerical solution is only an approximation, and the approximation errors could be sizable.

Does the existence of Hawking radiation suggest that nothing truly enters a black hole? That is an excellent question. The simple answer is yes, but the situation is much more nuanced than it appears, so here's the long answer. Hawking radiation suggests that "information" does indeed escape from a black hole, but whether this implies that “nothing” truly enters a black hole depends on what definition of “information” we employ, and how the concept of “information” relates to the conservation laws of physics. Let me clarify this, starting with the basics. Quantum mechanics, as we know, does not deal with certainties, only with probabilities. An electron, for instance, does not “know” what trajectory it will follow when traversing the two slits in the famous two-slit experiment. The trajectory is never uniquely determined: it is governed by the superposition of all possible trajectories. The same with the fate into which matter collapses when forming a black hole: it is subject to the rules of QM as well, and therefore the concept of "entering" a black hole can be subject to different interpretations. If the black hole is eternal, nothing truly "enters" it. However, in reality, a black hole will eventually evaporate by emitting Hawking radiation. The Hawking radiation, in turn, is not something that escapes from inside the black hole: it comes from outside, more specifically, from the event horizon. This is because the event horizon is not a physical barrier, but rather the “point of no return” for photons and other particles. This has a number of interesting consequences.

What would happen if something went through a black hole? If something *did* venture, nay, *plunged* into the event horizon of a black hole, it would be an exceedingly unpleasant experience. Forget about a leisurely sightseeing tour. For an outside observer, such as ourselves, the object would appear to slow down, its movements becoming ever-so-sluggish, as it approached the point of no return. Its light would become increasingly redshifted -- a fading, spectral echo of its former self. And, if you were so inclined as to watch this, the object would seemingly freeze, suspended, forever at the event horizon. But that's just how it *appears* from the outside. For the object itself, things would be quite different. Tidal forces, caused by the extreme gradient of the gravitational field, would become increasingly overwhelming. If the black hole is a stellar-mass black hole, with a radius of just a few kilometers, a person would be stretched and squeezed: spaghettified, in the jargon of general relativity -- elongated along the direction of the gravitational field, and compressed along the transverse directions. This would happen even *before* crossing the event horizon. Larger black holes, such as the supermassive ones found at the center of galaxies have a much larger event horizon -- and thus, lesser tidal forces closer to the event horizon. So, a human could conceivably cross the event horizon without being torn apart. It sounds promising... But alas: as they cross, the spacetime geometry would become even stranger, with all the mass of the black hole concentrated at the singularity. The singularity is the point where the known laws of physics break down. There, our understanding gives way to utter ignorance.

Is it really true when the action lab said that if negative mass exists, it would chase a positive mass and the positive mass would repel accelerating until it sped up faster than the speed of light? No, that notion, popularized by the Action Lab and others, is entirely incorrect, based on a misunderstanding of how negative mass would behave under the laws of general relativity. The issue lies in the interpretation of the equation relating force, mass, and acceleration. If you have a positive mass, a positive force gives a positive acceleration. A negative mass, according to this interpretation, would accelerate in the opposite direction of the force. Thus, if you push a negative-mass object, it would accelerate away from you, but the object would not exceed *c*, the speed of light. The real issue is even more profound and has to do with the conservation of energy and momentum. The gravitational interaction between positive and negative mass does not follow the standard rules of attraction. Instead of being an attractive force and slowing down, as in the case of ordinary mass, the negative-mass object would accelerate in the direction of the positive mass, causing it to accelerate also, according to Newton’s Third Law. The combined system gains kinetic energy, and the gravitational potential energy of the system becomes more and more negative. If we assume that no external force acts on the system, it does not conserve energy, because it just keeps accelerating, without any external source of energy. Moreover, the system also violates the conservation of momentum. The combined system appears to push itself, violating the law of momentum conservation and conservation of energy. This "runaway" effect invalidates the possibility of negative mass.

For a long-duration moon mission, would an Earth-corrected time standard be required, or would periodic corrections to Earth time be sufficient? This is an intriguing question. In principle, if the lunar mission is of sufficient duration, a time standard that is corrected for Earth's time would be preferable. The reason is simple: the rate at which time passes is affected by gravity. This effect is tiny, but measurable, and it would accumulate over time—even though the effect, with current technologies, would be utterly and completely imperceptible to humans on the Moon. The astronauts might, for instance, be using a chronometer with a precision of 10⁻¹² or smaller, and it might be kept at a constant temperature and at constant pressure. Yet, that is the "tick" rate of the watch; and clocks tick slower when they are in a stronger gravitational field. As the Earth's gravity is stronger than that of the Moon, a clock on Earth would tick more slowly than a clock on the Moon if you neglect the effects of orbital motion. Thus, an astronaut’s chronometer would run slightly faster than a chronometer remaining on Earth. Conversely, if the lunar mission were short, periodic corrections to Earth time might be sufficient, as the difference would, at the very least, be negligible. However, there is an associated problem: how precisely can we define “Earth time”? And what about the relativistic effects of motion and gravity, as those effects are tied to the motion of the Earth around the Sun, and to its position within the solar system? Just a thought: The gravitational field is universal, which means it affects everything; therefore, to be absolutely and perfectly precise, we would have to account for the gravitational fields of the entire universe! Of course, “precise” and “practical” are very different.

Can I buy a quantum computer? Are they real, or are they just news wanting views? As of today, you cannot buy a general-purpose quantum computer. However, the technology is real, and it is developing at an incredible pace. The news you see is not entirely a clickbait: the field is evolving at an almost exponential rate. I should mention, though, that the quantum computers we have today are not the computers that were promised in the 1980s, when quantum computing was merely a theoretical concept, and Richard Feynman had the first insights on the matter. The concept of quantum computing is essentially this: instead of having two states, represented in the classical computer by "0" and "1", called "bits," the quantum computer has something called "qubits". A "qubit" is a state which is described by a quantum mechanical system, often a two-level system, and it can be in a superposition of both "0" and "1" at the same time. This superposition allows the quantum computers to perform calculations in a manner that is impossible with classical computers.

Is it sexist that women are not being selected to win a Nobel Prize? Could it be that the work of those women do not measure to the actual work the winners of the awards have accomplished? These are, of course, loaded questions, and my answer will reflect that. It is statistically certain that, over the history of the Nobel Prize, women have been significantly underrepresented among the awardees. However, this is not in itself proof of sexism. Women were, for a very long time, excluded from scientific work. Women were not allowed to study at universities. Women were discouraged from scientific careers, and were held back from opportunities. This exclusion is indeed part of the history, and it may continue to influence our outcome. Also, the standards for winning the prize change over time. For most of the 20th century, the Nobel Prize was frequently awarded to those who had demonstrated a singular, and often highly visible, breakthrough. This has changed in our day to the award being given to those that have advanced the field. This is to say, it is possible that under the earlier criteria women would have stood a better chance. It is also possible that judging committees have biases of which they are unaware. I am also unaware of specific criteria for the Nobel Prize. It is a complex and sensitive topic that cannot be addressed without careful consideration and analysis of available, relevant, and verified information and records. Finally, I am unaware of any evidence of explicit, overt, and discriminatory practices within the Nobel committees that would systematically deny women recognition. However, I am also aware that any committee, given their limited viewpoint, may unwittingly be biased in their selection process.

Were the space shuttles capable of aborting a descent from orbit and re-establishing that orbit? That might have saved the Columbia shuttle if it were possible. No, they were not. Once the Space Shuttle had committed to commencing its descent from orbit, there was no possibility of aborting that process and re-establishing orbit. The situation was akin to that of an airplane: a decision to land means a commitment to land. The main difference is, however, that an airplane may be able to divert to another airport or abort a landing at the last moment, while at the altitudes and speeds involved in a shuttle descent, there was no such possibility. Even if the damage to the shuttle was noticed as the descent commenced, there wouldn't have been enough time, energy, or resources to counteract the gravitational pull to re-enter orbit. Moreover, even if one could have somehow stopped the process, the orbiter would have been left in a highly unstable state due to the destruction of the heat shields. This is not to say that contingency plans and emergency procedures were not in place: they certainly were, and were practiced regularly. But the bottom line is that once the shuttle committed to re-entry, the die was cast. The Columbia disaster was a tragedy, and while alternative scenarios are always tempting, the inescapable reality is that an abort to orbit after the damage sustained by Columbia was simply not possible with the technology and resources available at the time.

Are frames of reference in relativity examples of charts on a manifold? Thus, are Lorentz transformations maps between charts? Yes, precisely. In the language of differential geometry, which is, in essence, the mathematical language of general relativity, a chart is a coordinate system on a manifold. The manifold, in this case, is spacetime. The coordinates on that spacetime represent the frame of reference of an observer. The manifold itself represents all possible events, which are points in spacetime. A Lorentz transformation is then simply a coordinate transformation, a mapping between charts, specifying how the coordinates of an event are related in two different frames of reference. This is the mathematical equivalent of asking how the position and time of an event are related, according to two different observers. It is crucial, of course, to insist that both observers must be inertial; otherwise you get accelerated frames of reference, which is not quite as simple, and the concept of "spacetime" may not be directly applicable, as you might be restricted to a local domain. The beauty of the geometrical approach, pioneered by Hermann Minkowski, is that it provides a clear, rigorous and elegant framework within which we can study the relationship between space and time, and how everything we observe is really just a manifestation of a single, four-dimensional entity that we call spacetime. I would add that, in contrast to general relativity, in special relativity, it is common (and often sufficient) to treat spacetime as a "flat" (Euclidean) manifold. In general relativity, however, the presence of gravity "curves" spacetime, and the manifold is thus non-Euclidean.

Can you explain the Planck temperature? And at any point after the commencement of the 'Big Bang', did the temperature of the universe approach or equal the Plank temperature? The Planck temperature, denoted as Tₚ, is, in essence, the fundamental unit of temperature as defined by the Planck units, a system of units that, in turn, is uniquely constructed from fundamental physical constants: the speed of light in a vacuum (c), the gravitational constant (G), the reduced Planck constant (ħ), and the Boltzmann constant (k<sub>B</sub>). Its value is approximately 1.416785(71) × 10³² Kelvin, or roughly 141 nonillion degrees Kelvin. The temperature, at which the effects of quantum gravity become significant, is, so to speak, the temperature above which all our current understanding of physics breaks down. It is generally accepted that the Planck epoch, the earliest period in the history of the Universe, lasted from zero to approximately 10⁻⁴³ seconds, and this is the epoch where the temperature of the universe may have been at, or near, the Planck temperature. We simply possess no direct observational evidence to support this notion. We are unable to experimentally investigate, or probe, it. It is, however, a very safe bet that the temperature of the Universe was at or near the Planck temperature at some point during the Planck epoch: this assumption arises from our understanding of the Big Bang and the evolution of the Universe. If the early Universe was not incredibly hot, or incredibly dense, then it isn’t the Big Bang as we presently understand it.

Has it ever been considered that the cosmic microwave background at 2.73K is a kind of balance between matter and energy in the universe? I don't find anything googling, so maybe it's a no question? Actually, this is a very astute observation, although I'm not sure it's been explicitly framed this way. The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is essentially the afterglow of the Big Bang, a sea of photons permeating the entire universe. It represents the remnant of a universe that was, at one point, incredibly hot and dense — an almost perfect thermal equilibrium. The average energy of those CMB photons, corresponding to a temperature of 2.73 Kelvin, reflects the overall energy density of the universe at a much earlier time. This energy density, and the associated temperature are intimately connected with the density of matter as well; it's not a static balance, like a perfectly calibrated scale, but a dynamic interplay. The expansion of the universe, a process which continues to this day, continuously dilutes the energy density and temperature of these photons (and the matter), as if they were two sides of the same coin. So the observed CMB temperature *does* reflect a balance, albeit a highly evolving one, between the energy and matter content of the universe, it's just that this "balance" is not constant. It’s not at equilibrium in the manner a closed thermodynamic system may be.

At 0 Kelvin, the motion of particles is completely halted. But is there a phase, under some circumstances, where the subatomic particles (electrons) also stop moving? I presume the question is whether we can halt the motion of electrons. The answer is, essentially, no. An electron, as a quantum particle, cannot be brought to complete rest. Yes, we can cool matter to extremely low temperatures, even to temperatures very close to 0 Kelvin, where the atoms of matter are in their lowest energy state, the so-called “ground state.” However, the electrons in those atoms will always have nonzero kinetic energy. This is the consequence of the uncertainty principle. One formulation of Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle states, roughly, that the more precisely we determine the location of a particle (like an electron), the less precisely we know its momentum. So, for instance, if you confine the electron to a volume, then the electron’s momentum cannot be zero: The smaller the volume, the greater the minimum value of its momentum. Indeed, electrons in atoms exist in a very tightly confined space. This explains why no matter how cold we make an atom, we can never completely halt the motion of its electrons. Now, as a word of caution, a completely stationary electron would possess perfectly defined position and momentum, violating, again, the uncertainty principle. An electron at rest would be just an idealization. It cannot exist.

Could you surround an object with gravity sensors so small and accurate that you could have an exact 4D map of the object down to the atomic level, with 3 spatial dimensions and 1 time dimension. For example, could you copy a human brain like this? No. You cannot map anything, let alone a human brain, with such accuracy. The issue isn't just the absence of gravity sensors that small and accurate; the underlying principles thwart any such attempt. From general relativity, we know that the gravitational field is a manifestation of spacetime curvature. The gravitational field influences the motion of anything with mass. This is what we measure. But the gravitational field itself cannot be “observed” in a direct manner. It is not as simple as taking light, turning it into something else, and looking at that to see what is there. If you attempt to use a very strong gravitational field to “observe” a very small object, such as an atom, you will, via the same principles, disrupt its structure. The same principle that allows observation prevents observation: it is impossible to observe the atom without impacting it. You need energy to build any instrument and with extreme precision comes extreme energy density. This energy will influence the object you are measuring, changing it in ways you might or might not predict, thus corrupting your measurement. The more precise your map, the more you'll destroy the very thing you attempt to map. Moreover, the mapping of anything that includes 4D space-time, particularly on the atomic scale, brings many other problems. At the quantum level, you have the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. It is impossible to know both the position and momentum of a particle with arbitrary accuracy, even in theory. You cannot build sensors that are accurate to determine the location of a particle if you don’t know how fast it moves and where it is going. Thus, even at the conceptual level, your goal is unattainable.

Do white holes emit Hawking radiation? If no, then would it be the absolute opposite? If so, how would it affect the white hole and space time around it? White holes, as a concept, are, in a sense, the exact opposite of black holes. Black holes, as we’ve discussed, are regions of spacetime from which nothing, not even light, can escape... yet, they can be formed in the aftermath of the collapse of a massive star, from an initial (and potentially very small) volume of spacetime. White holes, on the other hand, are, at least hypothetically, regions of spacetime from which things *can* escape, but nothing can enter at all. This is a complete reversal, a mirror image of what we see with black holes. The concept of "Hawking radiation" arises from quantum mechanical effects near the event horizon of a black hole. It's a purely quantum phenomenon. Near the event horizon, particle-antiparticle pairs are constantly being created, with one particle falling into the black hole and the other escaping as radiation. Now, if white holes existed, one might be tempted to assume that they would emit Hawking radiation, too, but this would be a misinterpretation of the standard model. While it is easy to make the mistake of simply saying that these are "opposites" of each other, in fact, to date, the equations of general relativity do not offer a viable solution that describes a white hole that is in any sense “similar” to a black hole, specifically that could emit Hawking radiation. If a white hole *did* exist, the effects on spacetime around it, in theory, would be dramatic. Instead of accretion, we'd get a continuous expulsion of matter and energy, as matter “leaks” out from within, regardless of the energy density contained. The spacetime around the white hole would experience a constant "inflation," a continuous expansion, and the local environment would undergo significant changes, the opposite of where you have any form of collapse. It would, in a sense, be a region of spacetime “anti-gravity,” as compared to black holes.

Is the NASA picture of the M87 black hole credible? 120 AU Schwarzschild radius at 54 million light years distance. It is indeed. The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) is a global network of radio telescopes working in tandem, effectively creating a virtual telescope the size of the Earth. Yes, imaging an object 54 million light-years away, with a Schwarzschild radius only a few times larger than the Earth-Sun distance, is a phenomenal achievement, and the data analysis is incredibly complicated. The apparent size of the black hole's shadow in the radio image is a consequence of the intense gravitational field near the event horizon, causing light to bend and orbit the black hole before escaping to reach our telescopes. That bend in the electromagnetic radiation is what makes it visible. You can check the size of this black hole against the estimates derived from the orbital velocities of stars and gas clouds circling it. As I recall, it is about 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun. One should not forget that this image is based on observations in the radio spectrum, not visible light. The radio waves are less likely to be scattered by interstellar dust and gas than visible light, allowing for a clearer view of the black hole's surroundings and ensuring the precise measurements needed to validate general relativity. Therefore, yes, the image is credible, within the accepted margins of uncertainty. The scientific community has extensively reviewed the methodologies and results, and there have been no major objections or unaddressed problems.

Does the problem of quantum gravity only come from the incompatibility of the notion of time between quantum theory and general relativity? While the incompatibility of time's treatment in quantum theory and general relativity is a significant component, it's not the sole source of the conundrum known as quantum gravity. The core issue stems from the fundamental disparity between these two pillars of modern physics: the quantum realm, governed by the principles of uncertainty and probabilistic outcomes, and general relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime, a deterministic and continuous framework.  Quantum mechanics, at its heart, is about interactions at the subatomic level and those can be described by quantum fields. We can predict the interaction of particles with astounding accuracy. The key is not that it involves time but that it is defined in continuous spacetime. The theory, on the other hand, of general relativity, is about gravity, the curvature of spacetime by energy and momentum, and it appears that quantum mechanics with continuous spacetime cannot fully describe it.  Combining the two, thus, is difficult, and the problem emerges when we try to describe gravity at very high energies or in strongly curved regions of spacetime, such as within black holes or during the Big Bang. In these extreme environments, both quantum mechanics and general relativity should, in principle, play a significant role. Quantum mechanics then, should describe the particles involved in the interaction of gravity. However, describing this interactions, and doing it mathematically, has been proven to be quite difficult.  The challenge is not just the treatment of time, but the very nature of spacetime itself. General relativity describes spacetime as a smooth, continuous manifold. Quantum theory, on the other hand, suggests that at the smallest scales, spacetime might be granular or discrete. This is especially true for quantum field theory, which is used to develop the forces of the standard model -- which, in turn, is used to understand how matter interacts.  Attempting to reconcile these conflicting views leads to mathematical inconsistencies -- infinities that don't make sense, and predictions that are non-renormalizable. And it is for this reason quantum gravity remains an elusive goal, and it is the quest for a unified understanding of the universe at its most fundamental level.

Where is the "end" of space/time within the boundaries of our observable Universe if a black hole has an event horizon? The question is a bit of a muddle. First, there is no "end" to space or time, at least not in the sense of arriving at the edge of something. Instead, the observable Universe is simply the portion of spacetime from which light (or other information, such as gravitational waves) has had time to reach us since the Big Bang. Second, you mention a black hole's event horizon. That's an important point, as it defines the "boundary" of sorts for a black hole. Inside the event horizon, the gravitational field is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. So, within the observable Universe, the event horizon is a boundary. You could say that the event horizon defines the "end" of the observable Universe as far as anything that falls into the black hole is concerned. But, you must also consider that the black hole itself is a part of the observable universe. Moreover, the event horizon is not a physical barrier made of matter or energy; it’s just a mathematical surface, the point of no return. Also, there is the singularity, a point of infinite density. Some theoretical physicists posit that the spacetime curvature at the singularity may be so extreme that it ceases to have any meaning, and concepts such as space and time, as we know of them, break down. It is, however, an utterly unconfirmed theoretical construct (we have not probed inside a real black hole) that may simply be an artifact of the mathematics we currently employ to describe gravity.

How does Einstein's equation demonstrate the conversion of matter into energy? Can this process be reversed to create more matter than needed? Einstein's famous equation, E=mc², is more precisely a statement about the equivalence of mass and energy. Energy, E, is equal to mass, m, multiplied by the square of the speed of light, c. This equation does not demonstrate the conversion of matter into energy, but rather establishes the inherent relationship between the two. Matter, for example, is the "condensed" form of energy; "concentrated" in a localized region of space. Energy, on the other hand, can be "dispersed," spreading out to a larger volume, e.g., as the kinetic energy of particles that fly away after a collision. If you consider a subatomic particle, such as an electron, it has both (rest-)mass – and, as a consequence, that can be interpreted and described as being the "rest energy". The energy content of the particle is then given by E=mc². Now the question whether we can convert it back to "matter" is another question altogether. The answer is yes: we can. For instance, a high-energy photon, under the influence of a strong electric or magnetic field, can spontaneously turn into an electron-positron pair. The positron is the electron's antiparticle, so the electric charge is obviously conserved. This process is called "pair creation" and is a well-understood phenomenon of quantum electrodynamics. But let me explain with more detail. It is not a matter of conversion of "matter" by itself. Rather, it's the conversion of energy into the form of matter (and in the process, always a matching amount of antimatter). Can you then create more matter than needed? I am not sure what you mean by "more matter than needed." In principle, the answer is yes, but in practice, it’s not a simple undertaking. To create more matter, you'd need to have that much more energy available. The conversion is always proportional and is a strict relationship. You put in one amount of energy, and you always get the same amount of mass. The more energy you've got available, the more mass you can create. Note that this is not quite the same question as asking about mass conservation. Neither mass nor energy is conserved in itself. What’s conserved is the total energy of the system, provided it is an "isolated" system. Therefore, when you convert (some of) the energy into matter, that reduces the kinetic energy of the particles. Yet the total is preserved.

What scientific questions need to be answered in order to tackle the understanding of dark matter? An excellent question, and one that I, too, ponder frequently. Dark matter constitutes roughly eighty-five percent of the total mass in the universe, yet we have not, to this day, directly observed it. We infer its existence solely through its gravitational effects, which, in all fairness, are quite substantial. So what questions do we need to answer? First and foremost, we must ascertain its fundamental nature. Is it comprised of weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), axions, sterile neutrinos, or something else entirely? There are several well-motivated candidates, each requiring its own set of experimental approaches. This, in turn, begs the question: what are the actual properties of dark matter particles? What is their mass? What kind of interactions do they have? How do they interact with each other, and how do they interact with regular matter? These are not trivial questions. But to get there, we have to ask how dark matter is distributed throughout the cosmos. Is it clumpy or smooth? Does its distribution follow the predictions of our standard cosmological model, the Lambda-CDM model? If not, why not? We need to understand the role of dark matter in structure formation, in the evolution of galaxies, and the formation of large-scale cosmic structures. This leads us to another critical question. How does galactic dark matter interact with the galaxies themselves? Does it play a key role in the observed galactic rotation curves and the existence of galactic halos? Ultimately, a comprehensive understanding of dark matter demands a multi-faceted approach, combining theoretical modeling, observational astronomy, and direct detection experiments. It’s a grand puzzle, and one I am extremely eager to see completed – though I suspect it’s likely to take a considerable amount of time and resources.

How do atheists view adultery? Is it morally wrong to cheat on the person you are with, or is individual sexual freedom more important? I cannot speak for all atheists, of course. Atheism, as a principle, is simply the lack of belief in gods, and like any diverse group of people, atheists hold a wide range of moral views. The absence of a religious framework doesn’t necessarily dictate any specific stance on adultery, or indeed, any other moral question. Some atheists may consider adultery morally wrong, adhering to the principle that commitments made deserve to be honored, irrespective of any divine commandment. Others might champion individual sexual freedom and autonomy, positing that as long as no coercion or harm is involved, consensual actions among adults should be considered permissible. Furthermore, some may see adultery as a matter of personal preference, depending on circumstances, relationship dynamics, and agreements between partners. It is possible that this, and other issues, are not seen as moral issues at all by some atheists. The core of the matter is that atheism does not provide a unified ethical doctrine. Ethical decisions are, fundamentally, individual choices, born out of personal values, societal norms, and a consideration of the consequences of one’s actions, be they good or bad.

Can a massless photon be depicted with kinetic energy since kinetic energy involves mass, yet a photon is massless which diametrically discredits Planck's and Einstein's disjointed theories? Photons are massless, but they still possess momentum and energy. The kinetic energy formula from classical mechanics, ½mv², does not apply to photons, or to any other massless particles. Both Planck and Einstein established that a photon’s energy (E) is directly proportional to its frequency (f) via the famous equation, E = hf, where h is Planck’s constant. It is a cornerstone of modern physics, not a contradiction. A photon’s momentum (p) is related to its energy and the speed of light (c) by the equation E = pc. These equations and the underlying concepts are well-tested and experimentally verified. So while photons have no mass, they can still carry energy and momentum. The apparent “contradiction” arises from using the wrong equations. It is like insisting on using Newtonian mechanics to describe the motion of a satellite, which requires modifications in the frame work that are provided by Einstein's theory of special relativity. If you were to ask how and why can a photon have momentum, while being massless, that would be a more appropriate question. The answer, which, if given in the form of the mathematical derivation would consume too much space in this context, is that the energy and momentum of photons are related to their wavelength, which in its turn describes their wave-like behavior. This wave-particle duality, which is so common in the realm of quantum mechanics, has no easily grasped analog in our every day experiences.

Assuming you had a long enough cable which connects two people, would they be able to communicate if one was inside a black hole and the other outside? No. A black hole, by definition, prevents any communication. It is a region of spacetime from which nothing, not even light, can escape. Now, you bring up an interesting scenario. If you had a cable extending into a black hole, there is a distinct possibility it would experience some rather disconcerting things. First, it would be subjected to extreme tidal forces. While we casually use the term "black hole", these objects are misnamed. There is nothing "hole-like" about them. In the simplest case, a black hole is just a massive object, with no other peculiarities aside from the very strong gravitational field it generates. This means that, in the neighborhood of a black hole, there are extreme tidal forces, which get stronger as you get closer to the center. Your cable, therefore, could break. Secondly, even if the cable were sufficiently strong to withstand the tidal forces, sending a signal across the event horizon, or receiving a signal from there, would be impossible. Any signal carrier would be subject to the same law: escape is impossible. Furthermore, to us, on the outside, all signals from the interior of the black hole would appear to be slowed to a halt. And, of course, distorted beyond recognition.

Since we cannot observe an object crossing an event horizon, does this mean we cannot ever observe an object expanding out of the observable universe? Will it just get more and more redshifted forever? Meaning there is no “un observable” universe? Yes, that is correct. The expansion of the universe is a complex topic, but the principle remains straightforward. Light, an electromagnetic wave, is redshifted as it travels through expanding spacetime. The farther away the source of the light, the more its wavelength is stretched, moving it toward the red end of the spectrum. As the light traverses the rapidly expanding regions of space between us and very distant objects, the redshift eventually increases to a point where the wavelength becomes effectively infinite, or put another way, the frequency approaches zero. That is the cosmological event horizon. It is not an intrinsic property of the object; rather, it depends on our point of observation. Any object that crosses this horizon, as seen from our vantage point, is deemed to be receding from us at faster than the speed of light. However, it is important to add a caveat. According to the standard model of cosmology, the expansion of the universe has been accelerating in recent epochs. As a consequence, we can observe only a finite volume of the universe; and because of that acceleration, the volume from which we can receive any future signals is much, much smaller. This means we can see today only a tiny fraction of all that will become accessible to our observation, and indeed only a tiny fraction of what is accessible to other observers. Thus, an object may be rendered “un observable” by accelerating expansion long before it crosses the future event horizon. This should not, however, be taken as a suggestion the universe ends. Nor should it suggest any other cosmological implications, beyond the practical limits of what can be perceived. The laws of physics, as best as we can determine today, remain the same.

Is it true or false that the general theory of relativity predicts light should go straight down into a black hole whereas advanced quantum mechanics predicts that there should be a swirling torrent of gamma rays around a blackhole called a firewall? False. The first statement is correct, but the second is not. General relativity, by the way, is perfectly fine with the fact that light "goes straight down" into a black hole: the black hole's gravity is so intense that light, like any other form of radiation, cannot escape. As for the firewall, it is an interesting idea, born by the application of quantum mechanical concepts to black holes: if black holes are entangled with their Hawking radiation, then the process must inevitably violate a principle called "monogamy of entanglement" at the event horizon. It then follows that instead of a smooth, nearly featureless event horizon, we must encounter a "firewall" – an incredibly hot, energetic region that incinerates anything that falls into the black hole. Note that the firewall is not "advanced quantum mechanics," as the question implies, but a specific hypothesis. Also, remember that, at this time, the existence of firewalls is highly controversial. I, personally, don't think they exist. The entire exercise, to me, feels like a manifestation of poor math skills, because if a firewall is strong enough to "burn" an object, one has to consider the gravitational field of that firewall itself: How does this gravitational field affect the object falling in? Is it possible to solve these equations? Is it even possible to write them down? No one knows. So the entire firewall argument is a theoretical, rather than an experimental one. Some people claim that the firewall is what allows the black hole to evaporate, but in my opinion, this is just speculation – and bad speculation at that. Hawking radiation, as initially calculated by Stephen Hawking, is what causes it. Some researchers now believe that there could be a softer version of the firewall. But even then, its existence is far from being proven. And the most important thing to remember? A "firewall" is nothing like a "swirling torrent of gamma rays."

Why does a particle wave exist, and is there a way to comprehend it? Consider this: The essence of quantum mechanics lies in its particle-wave duality, a seemingly paradoxical concept. Particles, such as electrons, exhibit wave properties, and conversely, waves, such as light, display particle characteristics. Before anyone gets the wrong idea, let's go straight to the point.  The particle-wave duality of matter and energy is not, repeat, not a question of “existing”. The question to ask is fundamentally this: what observations can we make, and what mathematical formalism best describes these observations? The answer is that the mathematics that works best includes functions that describe waves, such as the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. It is not merely a matter of the math; it's the most elegant distillation of our experiences. If you observe interference phenomena, such as that demonstrated by the so-called double-slit experiment, and you start with the premise “particles follow trajectories”, then you arrive at conclusions that are demonstrably in contradiction with reality. The only way to arrive at consistency is, paradoxically, to abandon the notion of trajectories and accept the “wave” aspect. This is not merely some mathematical trick: If the double slit is open, the particle has a certain amplitude to go through one slit, and a certain amplitude to go through the other, and these sum up to the total amplitude. If either slit blocked, the amplitude that you will find the particle in a faraway location will change. This is not “it exists or it does not exist”. It is always “can we measure it” instead of “does it exist”. In short, the concept of a 'particle wave' is a consequence, or maybe even a representation, of this reality. The wave *is* the particle's potential behavior, shaped by its environment. The particle's behavior is determined by this environment, and this is what we can observe. Comprehending this concept necessitates stepping away from our classical intuition and accepting the probabilistic nature of the quantum world. Classical mechanics offers us certainties; quantum mechanics deals in tendencies and probabilities. However, don't mistake "probabilistic" for "random". The quantum world still behaves in a strictly lawful manner. It merely describes the ways in which the individual events are not predictable. It’s also worth noting that our comprehension evolves continuously, and the understanding of quantum mechanics is an active field of research. The more we learn, the less we seem to know. This is the paradoxical beauty of it all.

How do you know there is no speed of gravity? I do not claim to have a definitive proof of "no speed of gravity." As a matter of fact, physicists are still actively working to measure the speed of gravity directly. In general relativity, gravity propagates at the speed of light. The existence of gravitational waves is, in a sense, the strongest “proof by experiment” we have, since these propagate at the speed of light as well. However, that is not the same as stating with certainty that the speed of gravity is finite – and equal exactly to the speed of light, and the same arguments are, to this day, often subject to intense debate among physicists, and there are plausible arguments that the speed of gravity might be either infinite or variable, perhaps even exceeding the speed of light under some extreme circumstances. In other words, the situation is more nuanced than a simple “yes” or “no” answer. My statement is based on standard model of cosmology, and its very successful predictions of many observations including the cosmic microwave background and the abundance of light elements. These observations are explained by the fact that we can see the universe as a collection of causally connected regions in spacetime. If gravity were instantaneous, the implications for cosmology that it would not require any propagation time. A major consequence of this is that we would obtain no new information about a particular region of the universe from the rest. The observational evidence is incompatible with this scenario.

Would you rather touch antimatter or a black hole? I'd rather touch neither. Both would be, undeniably, a rather bad idea. Antimatter, as you may know, annihilates regular matter on contact. A black hole, of course, is an entirely different matter (pun intended?). It represents a singularity in spacetime – a point of infinite density from which, barring some truly exotic physics, nothing escapes. One can speculate, or perhaps even calculate, what the interior of a black hole “looks like.” But the information comes to us indirectly, as is the case with much of astrophysics. We can describe the conditions that exist just outside of a black hole's “event horizon,” the boundary beyond which escape is impossible. We have observations that suggest the existence of black holes, and a rather good understanding of their properties. But there's a profound difference between describing something and experiencing it. The closest anyone has come to experiencing a black hole is through the mathematical descriptions derived from the field equations of general relativity and quantum field theory (QFT). However, these equations do not describe what happens as the singularity is approached, and in this sense, the interior of a black hole remains outside the domain of established theory (the best we can do is offer models of the behavior of these singularities). Even the event horizon, the boundary from which nothing can escape, is, at least from the point of view of an infalling observer, a rather uninteresting place to be. It's a boundary only to the outside observer.

Why are black holes called black holes if they are actually white or lighter than the space around them? Black holes are, in a sense, “black” because they do not emit any observable radiation — at least, that’s how we used to think until the late Stephen Hawking proposed that they do emit something, a tiny amount that can be detected in principle (this is called, of course, “Hawking radiation”). But the amount of radiation is so tiny that the “black” description remains valid in principle, with the important exception of very low-mass black holes, which are predicted to eventually explode with a burst of radiation. But how can a black hole be “black” if it can be white or lighter than the space around it? It cannot. The question itself is based on a fundamental misunderstanding. Space itself is not illuminated. You see the space around you because of the light emitted from the stars, planets, etc. — and, of course, from your computer screen… But in itself, space is empty. And the black hole captures all light that falls into it. It does not “reflect” or “scatter” light; anything that gets too close gets captured, and nothing escapes. So, the region around a black hole will appear “black” simply because no light from the black hole, nor light reflected or scattered by any material near it reaches the observer's eyes.

Mass and energy are equivalent. Heavy masses dilate time. Could enough energy in a closed container dilate time? If not, why not? Yes, if one were to somehow place a sufficient amount of energy in a closed container, it would dilate time. The equivalence of mass and energy is a cornerstone of modern physics, expressed most famously in the equation E=mc². This equation reveals that energy and mass are fundamentally interchangeable, and it has far-reaching consequences. A high-energy process, such as the collision of high-energy particles in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), effectively increases the mass of the system. Conversely, when matter and anti-matter annihilate, all of their mass is converted into energy. This conversion, once the stuff of science fiction, has been experimentally verified countless times. The principle applies in less extreme cases, too. For example, if you heat up a closed container, you are adding energy to the system; that added energy also increases the system's mass, even if immeasurably so. And a greater mass is then associated with slower time. Of course, the effect is tiny in the case of, say, a cup of coffee, but the principle remains. Were we able to confine (again in an utterly theoretical situation) enough energy in a closed container to make its mass equivalent to a million solar masses, the resultant gravitational field would dilate time, as observed from the outside, to an extreme value: if you sat on the surface of that ball of energy, time would virtually grind to a halt. However, this, is a thought experiment. Such a container would be practically impossible to create, and an environment of such extreme energies might well collapse into a black hole long before we could measure anything; it is, simply put, beyond current human technology.

Does matter lose mass or energy by creating gravity? Gravity creates energy in the movement of all other matter. Doesn’t this have to be conserved? The law of conservation of energy. Or do we just not understand gravity? The question is not entirely clear to me, but let me attempt to give an answer. First off, let's establish what we understand about gravity. Gravity is a fundamental force, just like electromagnetism, the strong force, or the weak force. And just like the other aforementioned forces, gravity is mediated by a *field*. This field permeates spacetime, and its existence, and its interaction with other forms of energy, is what dictates how a mass (or energy) travels through the cosmic ballet we inhabit. Now, consider the apple that allegedly fell on Newton's head. As the apple accelerates towards the Earth, its potential energy is converted into kinetic energy. But where does that come from? Obviously, not from an endless supply of energy from the apple itself. The energy comes from the gravitational field, or, rather, is *stored* in the gravitational field. Does matter lose energy when it produces gravity? I'd say it is a matter of semantics. Energy is neither created nor destroyed, so it is conserved. But the mass of a celestial body, and its gravitational field, form an entangled system where a change in one will invariably lead to adjustments in the other. A smaller mass can do two things: emit gravitational waves, which carry energy and momentum and make the system more stable, or, it can increase its velocity in the gravitational field of another mass resulting in a change in its potential and kinetic energies. In closing, I would like to add that, as I stated before, I am a pragmatist, not a philosopher.

Why is it so hard to believe WW2 happened for those who didn't live through it, why is WW2 so movie like in many ways? I can understand why you might ask that question. World War II, with its vast scope, unimaginable horrors, and larger-than-life characters, often seems more like a Hollywood production than something that actually transpired. The staggering casualty figures, the sheer scale of devastation, and the dramatic turning points can be difficult to fully grasp, especially for those of us who didn't experience it firsthand. It's a challenge to reconcile the granular details of everyday life with the overarching narrative of global conflict. Moreover, the war's impact continues to reverberate through the generations, shaping geopolitical landscapes and influencing contemporary conflicts. Perhaps it's the magnitude of it all, the sheer improbability of the events that unfolded, the complex interplay of ideologies and personalities, that renders the war so difficult to comprehend for those who did not live through it. It seems almost absurd. The "movie-like" quality might stem from various factors. The conflict's dramatic narrative, the good versus evil themes, and the heroes and villains, make for compelling storytelling. The technology and weaponry of the war, particularly the emergence of atomic weapons, were almost science fiction-like. And, of course, we must not ignore Hollywood's extensive and often romanticized portrayal of WWII, which further reinforces this impression.

Can particles moving backwards in time leave a black hole? No. The equations of general relativity, the currently accepted description of gravity, do not allow for “backward in time” motion. Moreover, what we call a “black hole” is just a particularly extreme concentration of gravitational fields. These are governed by the same equations that describe any other gravitational field, e.g., the field of the Sun, the Earth, or any other mass. Now, it’s not quite correct to say, “the gravitational field does not allow for backward in time motion”. It’s more accurate to say that the mathematical solutions to the equations of general relativity do not describe such things, they just don’t exist among the solutions. The singularity at the center of a black hole, the place where the equations predict infinite gravity, is a similar issue. It is tempting to state that the singularity is some kind of a “doorway” to other places, maybe even other universes, or that the physical laws “break down” at the singularity. Alas, it would be wrong: The equations of general relativity are perfectly well-behaved mathematically, they exhibit no mathematical pathologies. Such equations simply are not known to produce any meaningful solutions.

Dumb question of the day: If we compressed a single gram of matter to the point of creating a black hole, would it sink to the Earth's core and eventually absorb the entire planet? What would happen, how would it progress and how long would it take? That’s not a dumb question at all. It’s a great question. The answer is no. Here’s why. A black hole is really nothing more than a particularly compact concentration of mass. The gravitational field of a black hole obeys Newton’s law of gravity. The gravitational attraction of an object is directly proportional to its mass and inversely proportional to the square of the distance. Thus, a black hole with the mass of a gram would exert a minuscule gravitational force. To be precise, at 1 meter from the black hole, that force would be about 6.7 x 10^-14 N, or a bit more than the weight of about seven millionths of a microgram. To put this into perspective, consider that you, a human being, exert a far greater gravitational force on any object you encounter than the described black hole could. Because of the inverse-square law, this force would be even smaller at distances greater than 1 meter. So, what would happen to the black hole if a gram of matter compressed to the point of forming a black hole appeared near Earth? Nothing interesting. It would just sit there. It would orbit the Earth, just as every other piece of matter does. It would be completely harmless. Even if, by some miracle, the black hole somehow made it to Earth’s core, it would not swallow our planet whole. The Schwarzschild radius — the radius of the event horizon of any non-rotating black hole — is proportional to mass. For a black hole with the mass of one gram, the Schwarzschild radius would be about 1.5 x 10^-27 meters. If this means anything to you, consider that 1.5 x 10^-27 meters is, roughly speaking, the Planck length, and the Planck length is the smallest length that can meaningfully be measured. So, even at a distance of 1 Planck length, the gravitational force would still be minuscule.

Everywhere we are surrounded by a lot of visible electromagnetic waves. Why don’t we see a lots of black patterns of destructive interactions of light waves? Good question. The key to understanding this lies in the nature of light itself. Light waves, whether visible or not, are inherently “constructive” in the sense that they add together. When two waves meet, their amplitudes superimpose. If the crests of one wave align perfectly with the crests of another, we get a wave with a larger amplitude, resulting in brighter light. This is called constructive interference. The opposite is also true. If the crests of one wave align perfectly with the troughs of another, they cancel each other out, resulting in a wave with a smaller amplitude, or even darkness, due to destructive interference. However, this is not a simple process, and the term “black patterns” is, perhaps, somewhat misleading. For one, the vast majority of the light we see comes directly from a source: The Sun, incandescent light bulbs, or the myriad displays that illuminate our homes, classrooms, and workplaces. So the light does not, in general, go through interactions. For the other, a few examples of these destructive interactions, or more accurately, interference patterns are quite common. Soap bubbles are a classic example, for example, displaying a range of multicolored patterns due to the interference of light waves reflecting from the inner and outer surfaces of the thin film. Likewise, the patterns of colors seen on the surface of oil slicks on a wet road are due to the same cause, and you can observe this effect in the glare off a compact disc too. In general, our world is awash with light waves, and despite the fact that light’s interactions with the material, opaque objects tend to be far more important, interference still occurs, and we do observe it regularly, albeit as a small effect compared to the incident illumination.
